title: Exploring Spousal Identity Theft and its Ramifications on Divorce Proceedings
excerpt: Spousal identity theft constitutes a particularly deceptive form of identity fraud, wherein one partner in a marriage illicitly utilizes the other's data without consent.

children.text: Spousal identity theft constitutes a particularly deceptive form of identity fraud, wherein one partner in a marriage illicitly utilizes the other's data, such as social security numbers, banking details, or credit card information, without obtaining prior consent. This act of betrayal not only undermines the victim's financial stability but also inflicts profound emotional distress and a pervasive sense of mistrust in relationships. The dissolution of a marriage often brings this type of deception to light, adding an intricate layer of betrayal and legal entanglements to the already challenging process of divorce.
Comprehensive Insight into Spousal Identity Theft

Spousal identity theft transpires when one spouse secretly exploits the other's credentials for purposes ranging from financial advantage to the deliberate sabotage of the partner's creditworthiness and standing. The intimate nature of the marital relationship often renders the victim's personal information readily accessible, facilitating such fraudulent activities.
Implications for Divorce Proceedings

The revelation of spousal identity theft can significantly exacerbate the complexities of divorce proceedings. Financial deceit injects additional discord and skepticism into negotiations concerning asset allocation, alimony, and child support. Moreover, it necessitates pursuing supplementary legal measures, encompassing criminal charges against the offender and civil litigation to alleviate the financial and reputational damage inflicted upon the victim.
Legal Dynamics:

Victims must navigate the dual legal landscapes of family law and identity theft legislation. This journey initiates with the daunting task of substantiating the theft, a particularly challenging endeavor given the commonality of joint financial ventures in marriages.
The Emotional Consequences:

The repercussions of spousal identity theft extend beyond mere financial detriment, engendering significant emotional turmoil. Victims often grapple with feelings of vulnerability, outrage, and a profound erosion of trust.
Ten Signs of Spousal Identity Theft
Discrepancies in Financial Disclosure:
Unexplained assets and debts in your spouse's disclosure can hint at financial activities conducted in your name without your consent.
Unfamiliar Debts During Asset Division:
The division of assets can uncover debts one spouse was unaware of.
Secret Accounts Come to Light:
Discovering secret bank or credit accounts in your name that were previously unknown.
Credit Report Anomalies:
New accounts, inquiries, or debts one spouse did not authorize.
Inconsistencies in Credit Card Statements:
Charges or accounts that a spouse does not recognize.
Disputes Over Debt Responsibility:
If your spouse insists certain debts are solely your responsibility, yet you have no knowledge of them.
Unexplained Financial Hardship:
Financial standing significantly worse than expected.
Unauthorized Withdrawals or Transfers:
Unauthorized withdrawals from joint accounts.
Sudden or Unexplained Changes in Lifestyle:
Spouse has access to financial resources that don't match their known income.
Legal or Collection Notices for Unrecognized Debts:
Receiving notices for debts you did not incur.
Strategies for Protection and Recovery
Immediate Reporting:
Alert credit bureaus about fraudulent activities and place fraud alerts on credit reports.
Evidence Compilation:
Amass all documentation indicative of the fraudulent activities.
Legal Counsel:
Engage attorneys well-versed in family law and identity theft.
Financial Decoupling:
Disentangle financial dealings from those of the spouse.
Credit Rehabilitation:
Dispute unauthorized transactions and debts with credit bureaus.
How a CDLP Can Help

A Certified Divorce Lending Professional (CDLP) is a specialized mortgage professional with additional training to assist individuals going through divorce with their mortgage and financial needs. A CDLP can help with:
Identifying Impact on Mortgage Financing
Strategic Financial Planning
Liaising with Legal and Financial Professionals
Guidance on Credit Repair and Debt Management
Educating on Mortgage Options and Rights
Navigating Post-Divorce Mortgage Challenges

title: The Primary Misunderstanding About Divorce Mortgage Planning with a Certified Divorce Lending Professional
excerpt: Divorce is a multifaceted process that involves not only emotional and legal considerations but also significant financial implications.

seo.metaDescription: Divorce is a multifaceted process that involves not only emotional and legal considerations but also significant financial implications.

children.text: The decree said she got the house. It said he was responsible for the mortgage. Both parties signed. Both attorneys were satisfied. Everyone went home.

Fourteen months later, he was late twice on that mortgage, and it appeared on her credit report — because she was still on the note. She couldn't refinance it out of his name because the settlement had defined the buy-out in a way that no lender would fund. And the support payments she planned to use as qualifying income hadn't been received long enough to count.
None of this was anyone's bad faith. It was a timing problem. The mortgage professional came in after the decree, and by then the decree was the constraint.
That's the primary misunderstanding: mortgage planning is treated as a post-divorce errand when it is actually a
term-drafting input
. The settlement language determines what financing is possible afterward. Get the language right and the financing follows. Get it wrong and no lender can fix it later.

I hold the Certified Divorce Lending Professional designation, which is a mortgage credential, not a legal or tax one. I'm not your attorney and not your CPA. What follows is general education about how financing rules interact with settlement terms — your attorney handles the law, your tax advisor handles the tax.
Trap One: The Deed and the Mortgage Are Not the Same Document
This is the single most common and most damaging misunderstanding in divorce lending.
The
deed
establishes who owns the property. In Oregon, a quitclaim deed can transfer one spouse's ownership interest to the other.
The
note and deed of trust
establish who is legally obligated to repay the debt.
Signing a quitclaim deed removes you from title.
It does not remove you from the mortgage.

Your lender was not a party to your divorce and is not bound by your decree. If your name is on the note, you owe the money — regardless of what the decree says, regardless of who lives there, regardless of who agreed to pay.
The consequences are concrete:
Credit exposure.
Every late payment reports on your credit for as long as you're on the note.
Debt-to-income impact.

That mortgage payment generally counts against you when you apply for your own financing. There are guideline provisions for excluding a payment assigned to an ex-spouse by a decree, but they have documentation requirements and they don't apply universally.
Total loss of control.
You carry the liability with no ability to affect whether it's paid.
There are exactly two clean ways off a mortgage:
refinance
into the retaining spouse's name alone, or
assumption with release of liability
, where the lender formally approves the remaining borrower and releases the departing one. Note the second half of that phrase. An assumption without a release of liability leaves you on the hook.

Most conventional loans are not assumable. FHA and VA loans generally are, subject to lender approval and the remaining borrower qualifying on their own. On VA loans, entitlement is a separate issue — a veteran's entitlement can remain tied to the property, potentially limiting their ability to use the benefit for a future purchase. That belongs in the negotiation.
Trap Two: Support Income Has Seasoning Requirements
The retaining spouse plans to qualify using spousal or child support. Reasonable — it's real income. But lenders don't count it just because a decree awards it.
Requirements vary by loan program and investor and do change over time, but the general framework is consistent:
A documented, court-ordered obligation.
The decree or support order must clearly establish the amount and the duration.
A receipt history.
Lenders commonly want to see that payments have actually been received for a period of time — six months is frequently cited, twelve for some programs — documented through deposits, not assertions.
Continuance.
The income generally must be expected to continue for at least three years past the loan closing. Child support for a 16-year-old typically fails this test.

Read those together and the timing problem becomes obvious. If a settlement requires the retaining spouse to refinance within 60 days of the decree, and their qualifying income depends on support they haven't received yet, the settlement has required something that cannot be done.
This is fixable — in the drafting stage.
A realistic refinance window, drafted with the seasoning requirement in mind, costs nothing to write and prevents the entire failure. Written after the fact, it's a modification.
Trap Three: Buy-Out Timing and Structure
When one spouse buys out the other's equity, the structure of that transaction determines how a lender treats it.
There's an important distinction in conventional guidelines between a
rate-and-term refinance
and a
cash-out refinance

. Buying out a co-owner's equity pursuant to a divorce can, under specific conditions, be treated as rate-and-term — which generally means better pricing and higher allowable loan-to-value than cash-out.

Those conditions typically include things like: the parties held joint ownership for a required period, the settlement documents specifically require the buy-out, and the departing spouse is removed from title at or before closing. The details are investor-specific and they change.
What this means practically:
the way your attorney words the buy-out provision can change which refinance category it falls into.
Precise language identifying the payment as an equity buy-out required by the settlement is not decorative. It's the difference between two different loan products.
Other timing items worth building into the language:
Who occupies the home at refinance closing
affects occupancy classification, which affects pricing and guidelines.
When the quitclaim deed records
relative to the refinance closing matters and should be coordinated, not left to chance.
A contingency if the refinance doesn't happen.
What occurs if the retaining spouse cannot qualify? A settlement without a fallback creates a second dispute. A sale trigger, a deadline, or a defined alternative belongs in the document.
The Oregon Layer

Oregon is an equitable distribution state. Marital property is divided in a manner the court finds just and proper, which is not a fixed formula. Because outcomes are negotiated rather than dictated, the specific terms carry real weight — and financing feasibility is one of the things those terms should be tested against.
A few practical Oregon notes:
Recording is county-specific.
Multnomah, Washington, and Clackamas counties handle recording separately, with different timelines. When a deed and a refinance need to record in coordination, this matters.
Oregon uses deeds of trust,
so the departing spouse's release involves a reconveyance rather than a mortgage satisfaction.
The Oregon Bond Residential Loan Program

may be relevant for a departing spouse purchasing a new home, depending on first-time buyer status, income limits, and county purchase price limits. Worth asking about rather than assuming disqualification — a person who owned a home with a former spouse may still qualify under certain circumstances.
Who Does What
Three professionals, three jobs, all at the same time:
Your attorney
negotiates and drafts the settlement and advises on the law.
Your CPA or tax advisor
handles basis, capital gains treatment, the tax character of support, and dependency questions.
Your CDLP
confirms whether the financing the settlement contemplates can actually be executed, and flags language that would prevent it.
The CDLP does not replace either of the others. The point is sequencing: all three involved while terms are being written, not one at a time afterward.
What to Do Next
Bring a mortgage professional in during negotiation,
before terms are drafted — not after the decree.
Ask your attorney explicitly
how and when your name comes off the mortgage, and confirm the answer is a refinance or an assumption with release of liability.
If you plan to qualify using support income,
get the seasoning requirements confirmed and make sure the refinance deadline is realistic.
Have the buy-out provision reviewed
for financing implications before it's finalized.
Ask for a fallback provision
covering what happens if the refinance can't be completed.

If you're in the Portland area and working through this, having the financing conversation early costs you nothing and can change the terms in your favor. This is general education only, not legal, tax, or individualized financial advice — take those questions to your attorney and your tax advisor.

faqs.question: If the divorce decree says my ex pays the mortgage, why is it still my problem?
faqs.answer: Because your lender wasn't a party to your divorce and isn't bound by the decree. If your name is on the note, you're legally obligated to the lender no matter what the decree assigns. Late payments will report on your credit, and the payment generally counts in your debt-to-income ratio. Only a refinance or an assumption with release of liability removes you.

faqs.question: I signed a quitclaim deed. Doesn't that take me off the loan?
faqs.answer: No. A quitclaim deed transfers your ownership interest in the property. It has no effect on the note, which is the document creating your repayment obligation. It's entirely possible to have zero ownership and full liability at the same time — arguably the worst position available. Removing the debt requires a refinance or a lender-approved assumption with release.

faqs.question: How soon can I use spousal support to qualify for a mortgage?
faqs.answer: Generally not immediately. Most loan programs require a documented history of actually receiving the payments — six months is commonly cited, twelve for some programs — plus a court-ordered obligation and an expectation that the income continues at least three years past closing. This is why the refinance deadline in your settlement needs to be drafted with that timeline in mind.

faqs.question: When should I actually talk to a mortgage person during a divorce?
faqs.answer: During the negotiation, before terms are drafted. The settlement language determines whether the financing it contemplates is achievable — refinance deadlines, buy-out structure, and how support income is documented all have loan guideline implications. After the decree is signed, those terms become constraints, and changing them means going back to court rather than editing a draft.

title: CDLP Divorce Mortgage Planning and Real Property Detail Report
excerpt: In a divorce, we are often more focused on curing the problem than understanding the full financial picture.

seo.metaDescription: In a divorce, we are often more focused on curing the problem than understanding the full financial picture.

children.text: A couple sits down to divide a house. They agree it's "worth about $600,000." They pull up an online estimate, subtract what they think the mortgage balance is, split the difference, and write it into the settlement.

Eight months later, one of them discovers the payoff was $18,000 higher than the statement balance, there was a HELOC nobody had thought about in years, and the county records a lien from a contractor who was never paid. The number they negotiated was fiction. The settlement is signed.
This is the problem a
Real Property Detail Report
exists to solve. It is not a document most divorcing homeowners have heard of, which is unfortunate, because it is one of the least expensive ways to avoid one of the most expensive mistakes.

A note before going further: I'm a mortgage professional holding the Certified Divorce Lending Professional designation. I'm not an attorney and not a CPA. Everything here is general education about the financing side. Legal questions go to your attorney; tax questions go to your tax advisor. Those are not disclaimers for form's sake — the mortgage piece touches the legal and tax pieces constantly, and you need all three.
Why "About What It's Worth" Is Not a Number
Home equity feels like simple arithmetic. Value minus what you owe. In a divorce, nearly every term in that equation is softer than people assume.
Value

is not one number. There's an online automated estimate, a real estate agent's opinion of value, a formal appraisal, and a lender's appraisal for financing purposes — and they routinely disagree. Which one governs your settlement should be a deliberate choice, stated in writing.
What you owe

is not your statement balance. The payoff figure includes accrued interest through the payoff date, and may include recording fees, reconveyance fees, and in some cases a prepayment consideration. It is nearly always higher than the balance printed on the statement.
Net proceeds

are not equity. Whether the house is sold or bought out, there are costs: agent commissions if sold, closing costs, Oregon's transfer and recording fees, escrow charges, and any liens that must clear.
Guessing at any one of these produces a settlement that's wrong. Guessing at all three produces one that isn't close.
What a Real Property Detail Report Contains
The report assembles, in one place, the verifiable facts about the property that a settlement should be built on. Contents vary by preparer, but a thorough report generally covers:
Ownership and Title
Vesting
— exactly how title is currently held, and in whose names
The recorded deed history for the property
Whether the vesting matches what both parties believe it to be, which is not always the case
Every Lien Against the Property
The first mortgage, with lender, loan type, origination date, and current terms
Any second mortgage, HELOC, or home equity loan — including HELOCs with a zero balance but an open, drawable line
Non-mortgage liens:
judgments, tax liens, mechanic's liens, HOA liens, and solar or PACE-type financing that attaches to the property

That third category is where the surprises live. A judgment lien recorded against one spouse can attach to jointly held real property, and it has to be resolved before the property can be refinanced or sold cleanly.
Loan Detail
Current principal balance versus
estimated payoff
, which are different numbers
Interest rate, loan type, and remaining term
Whether the loan is assumable — most conventional loans are not, but FHA and VA loans generally are, subject to lender approval and qualification
Whether mortgage insurance is present and under what terms
Property and Value Context
Legal description, parcel number, and county records data
Assessed value and current property tax status, including whether taxes are current
Recent comparable sales context for the specific neighborhood
Why This Changes the Negotiation
Once both parties are looking at the same verified numbers, several conversations get simpler.
The buy-out amount becomes calculable.
If one spouse is keeping the house, the equity to be divided can be computed from a real payoff, real liens, and a defined value — not from an estimate.
Financing feasibility becomes testable.

The critical question is whether the spouse keeping the home can actually qualify for a loan large enough to accomplish the buy-out. If the report shows a first mortgage plus a forgotten HELOC, the required new loan may be considerably larger than anyone assumed — and may not be achievable. Better to learn that before the settlement is drafted than after.
Hidden obligations surface early.
A tax lien or judgment discovered during the negotiation is a problem to be allocated. Discovered during the refinance, it's an emergency with a deadline.
Assumability gets evaluated properly.

If the existing loan is FHA or VA and assumable, that is a materially different set of options than a refinance. VA loans carry an additional layer: entitlement. A veteran whose entitlement stays tied up in a home the ex-spouse keeps may be unable to use their VA benefit again. That deserves explicit attention, not an assumption.
The Oregon Context
Oregon is an
equitable distribution

state. Marital property is divided in a manner the court considers just and proper, which does not mean automatically 50/50. There's a presumption of equal contribution to marital assets, but the outcome depends on the circumstances of the case, and how your attorney frames it matters.

Practically, that makes accurate numbers more important, not less. When division isn't a fixed formula, the negotiation carries more weight — and a negotiation built on wrong numbers produces a wrong result regardless of how the law would have applied.
A few local specifics:
County records differ.

Multnomah, Washington, and Clackamas counties each maintain their own recording systems with different search interfaces and turnaround. A property in Lake Oswego and one in Gresham require different lookups.
Property tax situations vary.
Oregon's Measure 50 assessed value system means assessed value and market value can be dramatically different for the same property. Do not use assessed value as a proxy for market value.
Trust deeds, not mortgages.
Oregon primarily uses deeds of trust, which affects how reconveyance works when a loan is paid off.
Timing: Pull It Early
The single most common mistake is ordering this information after the settlement terms are already agreed.

The report is most valuable during discovery and negotiation, while the terms are still being written. That's when a discovered lien can be allocated, an unrealistic buy-out can be restructured, and a refinance timeline can be built into the language rather than bolted on afterward.

Your attorney is negotiating the settlement. Your CDLP is confirming the property numbers are real and that the financing contemplated by the settlement can actually be executed. Those are different jobs, and they need to happen at the same time.
What to Do Next
Request a Real Property Detail Report early
— during discovery, not after terms are drafted.
Order an actual payoff statement
from the servicer, not just a monthly statement. Note its expiration date.
Decide with your attorney which valuation governs
the settlement, and write that definition into the agreement.
Bring the report to your attorney and your mortgage professional together,
so the legal language and the financing plan are built from the same facts.
Take tax questions to your CPA.
Basis, capital gains exclusion, and the treatment of transfers between spouses incident to divorce are real considerations, and they are not a mortgage professional's call.

If you're working through a divorce in the Portland area and want the property numbers verified before you negotiate, that's a conversation worth having early. This article is general education, not legal, tax, or individualized financial advice.

faqs.question: Can't I just look up my house value online and use that?
faqs.answer: You can, but you shouldn't build a settlement on it. Automated estimates are statistical models with wide error ranges, and they don't know about your remodel, your foundation issue, or your specific block. More importantly, value is only one of three variables — payoff amount and recorded liens are the other two, and no online tool shows you those.

faqs.question: What's the difference between my mortgage balance and my payoff?
faqs.answer: Your payoff is almost always higher. The statement balance is principal as of a past date; the payoff adds interest accrued through the actual payoff date plus administrative items like recording and reconveyance fees. On a large balance the difference can run into the thousands. Payoff statements also expire, usually within 10 to 30 days.

faqs.question: Who orders the Real Property Detail Report — me, my attorney, or the lender?
faqs.answer: Typically a mortgage professional with divorce lending training prepares it, often at the request of you or your attorney. It's not a standard part of a divorce filing, so nobody will produce it automatically. Ask for it during discovery, while settlement terms are still being negotiated rather than after they've been agreed to.

faqs.question: We already signed our settlement. Is it too late for this to help?
faqs.answer: It's still worth doing, but your options narrow considerably. Once terms are signed, discovering an unexpected lien or an unachievable buy-out amount usually means going back to your attorney about modifying the agreement, which is slower and more expensive than getting it right the first time. Run the numbers now rather than at the refinance application.

title: Mortgage This: 5 Tips for Working With Mortgage Brokers
excerpt: Did you know traditional financial institutions provide only 1/3 of all mortgages?

children.text: Every so often a client tells me they're going to "just check with their bank first," in the tone of someone doing the responsible thing. It is a reasonable instinct. It is also, frequently, how people end up comparing one option against zero options and calling it shopping.

To be transparent: I'm a loan officer. I have an obvious interest in how you read the next 1,200 words. So I'm going to try to be genuinely even-handed about where brokers help, where they don't, and where a bank or credit union is simply the better call.
Tip 1: Understand What You're Actually Choosing Between
There are three broad channels, and they differ in a way that matters.
Banks and Direct Lenders

A retail bank lends its own money using its own products. You get one menu. The upside is real: existing relationship, sometimes relationship pricing, and everything under one roof. If you have significant assets at a bank, ask what they'll do for you — sometimes the answer is meaningful.
The limitation is also real. If your file doesn't fit that bank's guidelines, there's no second option to try. The answer is just no.
Credit Unions

Credit unions are member-owned nonprofits, which changes their incentives in ways that show up in pricing and fees. Oregon has a strong credit union presence, and for straightforward W-2 borrowers with good credit, a local credit union is frequently very competitive. Some hold loans in portfolio, which can mean flexibility on files the secondary market wouldn't touch.
The tradeoffs: membership requirements, generally narrower product menus, and technology that can be less polished. Also, "nonprofit" does not mean "cheapest." Compare anyway.
Mortgage Brokers
A broker doesn't lend money. A broker is licensed to submit your file to multiple wholesale lenders and place it with whichever one fits best on price, guidelines, or turn time.
Where this genuinely helps:
when your file has a wrinkle.

Self-employment. Recent job change. Commission or bonus income. A non-warrantable condo. Anything where one lender's guideline says no and another's says yes. A broker can shop the file without you re-applying five times.
Where it helps less:
when your file is completely vanilla.
A W-2 borrower with a 780 score, 20% down, buying a single-family home in Hillsboro will get competitive offers almost anywhere. The broker's advantage narrows.
Tip 2: Know How Your Loan Officer Gets Paid
This is the question most people are too polite to ask, and it's the most useful one.
Under federal rules established after 2010, loan originator compensation cannot vary based on the
terms
of your loan. A loan officer cannot legally be paid more for steering you into a higher rate. That protection is real and it's worth knowing you have it.
Compensation generally works one of two ways in the broker channel:
Borrower-paid
— you pay the broker directly, disclosed as a line item on your Loan Estimate.
Lender-paid
— the wholesale lender pays the broker, at a percentage set in advance and applied uniformly to all that broker's loans with that lender.
Under lender-paid compensation, the broker's percentage is fixed in advance. They cannot raise it on your file specifically.

At a bank, your loan officer is typically a salaried or commissioned employee, and their compensation is embedded in the bank's pricing rather than disclosed separately. Neither model is inherently more honest. But you should know which one you're in.
Ask directly:
"How are you compensated on my loan, and is it borrower-paid or lender-paid?" Anyone who gets cagey about this has told you something.
Tip 3: Ask Questions That Actually Produce Information
Most borrower questions are too vague to be useful. "What's your rate?" produces a number attached to no assumptions, which you cannot compare to anything.
Better questions:
"Can I have a Loan Estimate?"
This is the standardized federal disclosure. It's the only apples-to-apples comparison tool that exists. Get them from two or three lenders within a short window.
"What's your typical turn time from application to clear-to-close, right now?"
In a competitive offer situation this can matter more than a small pricing difference.
"What could make this loan fall apart?"
A good originator will name the actual risks in your file. Someone who says "nothing, you're all set" is either not paying attention or managing you.
"Who underwrites this, and who will service it?"
Tells you whether decisions happen in-house and where your payments will go.
"What's your lock policy — length, cost to extend, and what happens if rates improve?"
Float-down provisions vary widely.
On Credit Inquiries

People avoid shopping because they're worried about their credit score. Multiple mortgage inquiries within a standard shopping window — typically 14 to 45 days depending on the scoring model — are generally treated as a single inquiry. Shop within a compressed window and the effect is minimal.
Tip 4: Have Your Documents Ready Before You Start
The biggest single cause of a stressful mortgage process is document lag. Not rates. Not underwriting. Paperwork you meant to send Tuesday.
Standard package for a W-2 borrower:
Two years of W-2s and two years of federal tax returns, all schedules
Most recent 30 days of pay stubs
Two months of statements for every account you'll use for down payment or reserves —
every page
, including the ones that say "this page intentionally left blank"
Photo ID
Current mortgage statement, homeowners insurance declarations, and HOA information if applicable
If you're self-employed, add two years of business returns, a year-to-date profit and loss statement, and K-1s or business licenses as applicable.
Two things that reliably create problems:
large deposits
that aren't payroll, and
gift funds
. Any non-payroll deposit needs a documented source. Gift funds need a signed gift letter and a paper trail from the donor's account. Handle both before underwriting asks.
Tip 5: Recognize the Red Flags
Not everyone in this industry is good at it. Watch for:
Verbal quotes with no written disclosure.
If someone quotes a rate and won't put a Loan Estimate behind it, the number isn't real.
Pressure to skip shopping.
"Rates are moving, sign today" is sometimes true and always a pressure tactic when used as the primary argument.
Reluctance to explain fees.
Every line on a Loan Estimate has a name and a reason. You're entitled to both.
Suggesting you not disclose something.
Any originator who hints at omitting a debt, misstating occupancy, or papering over a deposit is proposing mortgage fraud, and you'd be the one signing it.
No NMLS number.
Every licensed originator has one. Mine is 1367416. You can verify any originator at the NMLS Consumer Access site, and you should.
The Honest Tradeoffs

Brokers are not automatically better. They add a layer, their wholesale partners' service quality varies, and a bad broker is worse than a good bank loan officer. Banks are not automatically worse. If your bank's product fits and their pricing is competitive, take it.
The real differentiator is the individual person managing your file and how many options they can reach when something goes sideways. Shop the person as hard as you shop the rate.
What to Do Next
Get Loan Estimates from at least two channels
— ideally a broker and a bank or credit union — within the same week.
Compare page 2 line by line,
especially section A (origination charges), before you look at the rate.
Verify every originator's NMLS number
at NMLS Consumer Access.
Assemble your document package now,
before you're under contract and short on time.
This is general education, not advice on your specific situation. If you want a look at your actual numbers, that's a conversation.

faqs.question: Do mortgage brokers charge more than going straight to a bank?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily — brokers access wholesale pricing, which is generally lower than the retail pricing a bank quotes directly. Broker compensation is disclosed on your Loan Estimate as either borrower-paid or lender-paid. The only way to know which channel comes out ahead for your file is to get Loan Estimates from both and compare section A line by line.

faqs.question: Will shopping around hurt my credit score?
faqs.answer: Minimally, if you compress your shopping into a short window. Credit scoring models treat multiple mortgage inquiries within a standard shopping period — typically 14 to 45 days depending on the model — as a single inquiry. The far bigger risk is not shopping at all and having no comparison for the terms you're offered.

faqs.question: What's the one question I should ask a loan officer?
faqs.answer: "Can I have a Loan Estimate?" It's the standardized federal disclosure form, and it's the only genuinely comparable document across lenders. Verbal rate quotes carry no assumptions, no fees, and no accountability. A close second: "How are you compensated on this loan?" Both answers tell you a lot about who you're working with.

faqs.question: How do I check that a loan officer is actually licensed?
faqs.answer: Look up their NMLS number at the NMLS Consumer Access website, which is free and public. Every licensed mortgage loan originator in the country has one, and it should appear on their business card, email signature, and website. The site shows license status, states of licensure, and any regulatory actions on record.

children.text: Six weeks after closing on a house in North Portland, a client got a letter telling him his mortgage had been sold to a company he'd never heard of, in a state he'd never visited. He called me, genuinely upset, convinced something had gone wrong.

Nothing had gone wrong. That letter is one of the most normal events in American mortgage finance, and it happens to millions of people a year. But almost nobody explains the system beforehand, so it lands like bad news.

The mortgage market is not one business. It is four or five different businesses stapled together, and understanding who does what makes the whole process far less mysterious — and makes you much harder to take advantage of.
The Players
The Originator

This is who you talk to. A loan officer at a bank, a credit union, an independent mortgage broker, or a mortgage banker. Their job is to figure out what you can qualify for, help you choose a loan product, collect your documentation, and shepherd the file to closing.
Originators are salespeople in the useful sense — they are the interface between you and a complicated machine. A good one translates. A bad one just collects paperwork.
The Underwriter
The underwriter decides whether the loan gets approved. You will likely never speak to this person. They evaluate four things, usually described as the pillars of underwriting:
Credit
— your history of repaying debt
Capacity
— your income relative to your obligations, expressed as debt-to-income ratio
Capital
— your down payment, reserves, and where those funds came from
Collateral
— the property itself, established by appraisal

The underwriter's loyalty is to the loan guidelines, not to you and not to your loan officer. That is a feature. It is also why "my lender said I was pre-approved" and "the underwriter approved my loan" are different statements.
The Investor
Here is the part most borrowers never learn: the entity that funds your loan at closing usually does not keep it.
Most conventional loans are sold to
Fannie Mae
or
Freddie Mac
, government-sponsored enterprises that buy loans meeting their guidelines and package them into mortgage-backed securities. FHA and VA loans typically flow through
Ginnie Mae
. Loans that don't fit those boxes — jumbo loans, certain self-employed borrower profiles — are sold to private investors or held on a bank's own balance sheet as portfolio loans.
This is why guidelines exist and why they are not negotiable. Your loan officer cannot waive a Fannie Mae requirement any more than a cashier can waive sales tax.
The Servicer

The servicer is who you actually pay every month. They collect your payment, manage your escrow account, pay your property taxes and insurance, send your year-end statements, and handle you if you fall behind.
Servicing is a separate business from lending, with separate economics.
The right to service your loan is bought and sold independently of the loan itself.
This is the single fact that explains most of the confusing mail you get after closing.
What Actually Happens After You Close
Roughly, in order:
You sign at closing, typically at an escrow company here in Oregon rather than at an attorney's office as in some states.
Funds disburse, the deed records with the county, and you own the house.
Within days to weeks, the loan is sold to an investor or delivered into a securitization pool.
Servicing is assigned — sometimes retained by the original lender, often transferred to a dedicated servicer.
You receive a
servicing transfer notice
. Federal law requires notice, generally 15 days before the transfer takes effect, from both the old and new servicer.
Why Your Servicer Changes
Servicing rights are an asset with a market price. Companies buy and sell them for the same reasons companies buy and sell anything: portfolio strategy, capital needs, scale efficiency.
The important protections for you:
Your loan terms cannot change.
Rate, term, balance, and payment schedule are set by your note. A servicing transfer does not touch any of it.
You get a 60-day grace period.
If you accidentally send a payment to your old servicer within 60 days of the transfer, it cannot be treated as late or reported as late to credit bureaus.
Your escrow balance transfers with the loan.

What you should actually do when you get a transfer notice: confirm it's legitimate by calling the *old* servicer at a number you already have, not the number in the letter. Then update your autopay. Mortgage transfer scams exist and they target exactly this moment.
Reading the Market Without Losing Your Mind

Mortgage rates are not set by the Federal Reserve, despite what every headline implies. The Fed sets the federal funds rate, which is an overnight bank-to-bank rate. Mortgage rates track much more closely with the
10-year Treasury yield
and, more precisely, with the yield on mortgage-backed securities.
Those move on inflation data, employment reports, and investor demand for MBS. Sometimes they move in the opposite direction from a Fed announcement, which confuses everyone.
Two durable ideas worth internalizing:
Rates are not a single number.

The rate you're offered depends on your credit score, loan-to-value ratio, occupancy type, property type, loan amount, and whether you pay points. Advertised rates almost always assume a highly specific borrower profile.
Rate and cost are a tradeoff, not separate items.
You can generally pay points to lower your rate or accept a higher rate in exchange for lender credits toward closing costs. Neither is inherently better. It depends on how long you'll keep the loan.
Oregon-Specific Mechanics
A few things work differently here than in the states your out-of-state relatives are calling from:
Escrow-based closings.
Oregon uses escrow companies and title insurers rather than closing attorneys. Your escrow officer is a neutral third party, not your representative.
Deeds of trust, not mortgages.
Oregon primarily uses trust deeds with a trustee holding title in trust. The practical effect shows up mostly in foreclosure procedure.
County recording differs.

Multnomah, Washington, and Clackamas counties each have their own recording offices, fee schedules, and turnaround times. Your escrow officer manages this, but it's why closing timelines can vary slightly across the metro.
The Oregon Bond Residential Loan Program

offers below-market-rate financing and cash assistance options for eligible buyers through participating lenders, administered by Oregon Housing and Community Services. Eligibility depends on income limits, purchase price limits, and the county. Worth asking about if you're a first-time buyer here.
How to Be an Informed Participant
The system is not designed to be adversarial, but it is designed around volume. Files that are organized and borrowers who ask clear questions move faster and hit fewer surprises.
Compare Loan Estimates, not quotes.
The Loan Estimate is a standardized federal form. Get them from multiple lenders on the same day and compare page 2 line by line. Verbal quotes are worth exactly nothing.
Ask who will service your loan
and whether the lender retains servicing. Some do. It's a reasonable preference.
Understand your lock.
A rate lock has an expiration date and extension costs. Know both.
Respond to documentation requests fast.
Underwriting conditions are the number one cause of delayed closings, and most of the delay is on the borrower side.
What to Do Next
Before you apply,
pull your own credit and check for errors. Disputes take time you won't have mid-transaction.
Gather documents early:
two years of tax returns, two years of W-2s, 30 days of pay stubs, two months of full bank statements — all pages, including the blank ones.
When you get a Loan Estimate,
read pages 2 and 3, not just the rate on page 1.
After closing, keep your closing package.
Your note, deed of trust, and Closing Disclosure will matter again — for a refinance, a PMI removal request, or a tax question.
If you want someone to walk through your specific file rather than the general shape of the system, that's what a conversation is for. This is education, not advice on your particular loan.

faqs.question: Why did my mortgage get sold to a company I've never heard of?
faqs.answer: Because loans and servicing rights are routinely bought and sold, and it says nothing about you or your loan. Most conventional loans are sold to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac shortly after closing, and servicing is often transferred separately. Your rate, term, balance, and payment schedule cannot change as a result. Only the payment address does.

faqs.question: Does the Federal Reserve set mortgage rates?
faqs.answer: No. The Fed sets the federal funds rate, an overnight rate between banks. Mortgage rates track the yield on mortgage-backed securities, which moves with the 10-year Treasury, inflation data, and investor demand. That's why mortgage rates sometimes move opposite to a Fed announcement — the market often prices in expected moves before they happen.

faqs.question: What's the difference between the person I talk to and the person who approves my loan?
faqs.answer: Your loan officer originates the file; an underwriter approves it. The loan officer gathers your documents, explains products, and advocates for your file. The underwriter, who you'll likely never speak with, evaluates it against investor guidelines and makes the actual decision. Pre-approval from a loan officer is not the same as underwriting approval.

faqs.question: How do I know a servicing transfer letter isn't a scam?
faqs.answer: Call your current servicer using a phone number you already have — from an old statement or their website — not the number printed in the letter. Legitimate transfers require notice from both the old and new servicer, generally 15 days ahead. And you have a 60-day grace period where a payment sent to the wrong servicer can't be reported late.

children.text: There's a version of this question that gets asked at dinner tables constantly: should we refinance into a 15-year, or just throw an extra few hundred a month at the loan we've got?

Both get you to the same place — a paid-off house, sooner. They get there at different costs, with very different amounts of risk, and the winner flips depending on one variable most people don't isolate.
Let's run actual numbers. Everything below is
hypothetical
. These are illustrative figures chosen to make the arithmetic clear, not rates or payments available to anyone.
The Starting Point

That's the case for refinancing. When there's a real rate improvement available, the refinance does something extra payments cannot: it reduces the interest rate applied to every remaining dollar of principal. Extra payments only reduce the principal.
Scenario Two: The Rate Gap Is Small or Nonexistent
Same homeowner, but now assume the best available shorter-term option is also a
hypothetical 7%

Nothing changed except the rate gap, and the answer reversed. The $6,000 in closing costs bought nothing, and the borrower paid interest on it for fifteen years.
This is the whole decision.
If refinancing meaningfully lowers your rate, it usually beats extra payments. If it doesn't, you're paying closing costs to buy discipline you could have supplied yourself for free.
Whether a meaningful gap exists depends on current market conditions and on the rate you're carrying — which is why nobody can answer this in the abstract.
Scenario Three: When You Can't Afford the 15-Year Payment
This is where a lot of real households land. The 15-year payment of $3,088 is out of reach, but $2,800/month is doable.

and finishes two years earlier, at an identical monthly outlay — with the added benefit that if income drops, the *required* payment is only $2,622.
The lesson: 15-year versus extra payments is a false binary. A longer refinance term with voluntary extra payments often outperforms both, because you get the better rate *and* keep the flexibility.
The Things the Spreadsheet Doesn't Show
Flexibility has real value
Extra payments are voluntary. Lose a job, have a kid, replace a roof on a 1940s house in Beaverton — you stop the extra payments and revert to your normal obligation.
A 15-year mortgage is a contract. That $3,088 is due every month whether or not the quarter went well. For a self-employed borrower or anyone with variable income, that's not a small consideration.
Refinancing requires qualifying

Extra payments require nothing but the money. A refinance requires underwriting: income documentation, credit review, an appraisal or appraisal waiver, and a property that supports the loan amount. Approval is never guaranteed for anyone.
If your income structure changed since you got the original loan, the refinance you're modeling may not be available to you at all.
Discipline is not free either

The extra-payment strategy depends on you making that payment every month for a decade and a half. Most people don't. Automating the extra payment through your servicer, as a separate scheduled principal-only transfer, closes most of that gap.
And confirm with your servicer that extra funds are applied to principal. Some default to holding them or applying them to the next payment, which does nothing for your payoff date.
A recast is a third option
If you have a lump sum — an inheritance, a bonus, proceeds from a sale — some servicers will
recast
the loan: you pay down a large chunk of principal, and they recalculate your payment over the remaining term at the same rate. Modest fee, no closing costs, no underwriting.
A recast lowers your payment without shortening your term. It's not for everyone, but it's rarely on anyone's list, and it should be.
Taxes and opportunity cost

Accelerating a mortgage payoff means less mortgage interest, which can affect itemized deductions. It also means money that isn't going into retirement accounts or an emergency fund. Whether paying off a fixed-rate mortgage early beats the alternatives is a personal financial question — worth raising with a tax professional or financial advisor rather than a loan officer.
A Decision Framework
Find your rate gap.
Compare your current rate to what's realistically available for a shorter term today. That gap is the primary variable.
Calculate closing costs as a percentage of the benefit.
If the total interest savings from refinancing barely exceed the costs, extra payments are simpler and safer.
Stress-test the payment.
Could you make the 15-year payment through six months of reduced income? If not, don't sign up for it.
Consider the hybrid.
Refinance to a term you can comfortably afford, then pay it like a shorter one.
Confirm there's no prepayment penalty
on your current loan. Most modern mortgages don't have one, but check the note rather than assuming.
What to Do Next
Pull your mortgage statement and note your
balance, rate, and remaining term
— you can't run any of this math without those three numbers.
Use any online amortization calculator to model your current loan with an extra $200, $400, and $600 per month. Write down the payoff dates.
Ask a licensed loan officer for a Loan Estimate on a 15-year and a 20-year, and compare total interest against those extra-payment results.
Pick based on the total-cost comparison and your honest read of your own income stability — not on which one sounds more disciplined.
The right answer here isn't universal, and it isn't permanent. It moves with the rate gap and with your life.

faqs.question: Is a 15-year mortgage a better deal than just paying extra on my 30-year?
faqs.answer: It depends almost entirely on the rate gap. When a shorter-term refinance meaningfully lowers your rate, it typically beats extra payments because it reduces the interest applied to every remaining dollar. When the rate is similar to what you already have, closing costs usually make extra payments the cheaper route. Run both before assuming the shorter term wins.

faqs.question: Will my lender actually apply extra money to principal?
faqs.answer: Only if you tell them to, in most cases. Many servicers apply unlabeled extra funds to the next scheduled payment or hold them in suspense, neither of which shortens your loan. Set up a separate recurring principal-only payment through your servicer's site, then verify on the following statement that your balance dropped by the full amount.

faqs.question: What is a mortgage recast and how is it different from refinancing?
faqs.answer: A recast re-amortizes your existing loan after a large principal payment, keeping the same rate and payoff date but lowering the payment. There is no new loan, no underwriting, and no closing costs beyond a modest fee. A refinance replaces the loan entirely and can change the rate and term. Not all loans or servicers allow recasting, so ask before planning around it.

faqs.question: Should I pay off my mortgage early or invest the money instead?
faqs.answer: That is a personal finance question rather than a mortgage question, and it turns on your rate, your tax situation, your risk tolerance, and what other savings you have. Paying down a mortgage returns exactly your loan's interest rate with no market risk, while investing carries risk and an uncertain result. A tax professional or financial advisor is the right person to weigh those against each other.

title: What Are Mortgage Points and How Do They Affect Interest Rates
excerpt: If you're preparing to buy a house, you know there's a lot to learn about mortgage financing.

seo.metaDescription: If you're preparing to buy a house, you know there's a lot to learn about mortgage financing.

children.text: One discount point on a hypothetical $400,000 loan costs $4,000. That is the entire concept, mechanically. You hand over money at closing, and in exchange the lender lowers the interest rate on your loan.

What that $4,000 buys in rate reduction changes constantly. It varies by loan program, credit profile, loan-to-value, property type, and what the bond market did that morning. Anyone who tells you a point always lowers your rate by a fixed amount is describing a market that does not exist.
So the useful question is never whether points are good. It is whether prepaying interest is a better use of your cash than the alternatives, given how long you will keep the loan.
What A Point Actually Is
A point equals 1 percent of the loan amount. Not the purchase price, the loan amount. On a hypothetical $600,000 loan, one point is $6,000. Half a point is $3,000.
You can buy points in fractions. Most rate sheets are priced in eighths, so you might see options at 0.375 points, 0.75 points, and so on. You are not limited to whole numbers.
Economically, a discount point is
prepaid interest

. You are paying some of your future interest cost today in exchange for a smaller rate applied across the whole term. The lender is not doing you a favor and is not gouging you. It is a present-value trade, and both sides have run the math.

The reason this confuses people is that points get bundled into a broader conversation about closing costs, where a lot of unrelated fees live. Points are the one line item that directly buys you something measurable and ongoing.
Discount Points, Origination Points, And Lender Credits
Three different things wear similar names.
Discount points
buy down your interest rate. Optional. This is what people mean when they say points.
Origination points or origination fee
is compensation for making the loan. It does not lower your rate. It is a cost of doing business with that lender, and it belongs in your comparison of total costs.
Lender credits
are points in reverse. You accept a higher interest rate, and the lender gives you money toward closing costs. Sometimes called negative points.

That last one deserves more attention than it gets. If you are short on cash but have solid income, taking a higher rate in exchange for a credit that covers closing costs can be the difference between buying now and buying later. And unlike a down payment, a rate is not permanent. You can refinance a rate. You cannot un-spend cash.
When you compare offers from two lenders, compare them at the
same rate

. A quote with a low rate and two points is not comparable to a quote with a higher rate and no points until you normalize them. Page 2 of the Loan Estimate shows points explicitly in section A. Look there.
The Breakeven Calculation
Here is the arithmetic, using clearly hypothetical figures.

Suppose a buyer takes a hypothetical $400,000 loan. Scenario A is a hypothetical 6.5 percent rate with no points. Scenario B is a hypothetical 6.25 percent rate for one point, or $4,000. These numbers are illustrative only and are not quotes.
Calculate the monthly principal and interest under each scenario.
Subtract to get the monthly savings.
Divide the cost of the points by the monthly savings.
That quotient is your
breakeven month

. If the difference in this hypothetical came out to about $65 per month, the breakeven would land around 61 months, or roughly five years. Keep the loan longer than that and the points came out ahead. Sell or refinance sooner and they did not.
Two refinements make this more honest:
After-tax comparison.

Mortgage interest deductibility and the treatment of points depend on your situation. Points on a purchase of a primary residence are treated differently from points on a refinance. Ask a tax professional rather than assuming.
Opportunity cost.
The $4,000 could have gone somewhere else. If it would otherwise sit in a savings account, the comparison is simple. If it would otherwise pay off a credit card, the credit card usually wins.
Also note that the breakeven is calculated on principal and interest only. Taxes and insurance do not change when you buy points, so do not include them.
The Three Questions That Decide It
Skip the spreadsheet for a moment. Three questions do most of the work.
How long will you keep this exact loan?

Not how long will you own the home. How long will this loan survive. Those differ, because refinancing kills the loan while you keep the house. If you expect to refinance, points bought today may not live long enough to pay off.
Do you have the cash without touching your reserves?

Paying points with money you needed for an emergency fund converts a liquid asset into an illiquid one. That is a real risk, not a theoretical one, especially on an older Portland home where the sewer line is a genuine plot point.
Is your rate locked into a long horizon by circumstance?
A borrower planning to stay in a Southeast Portland bungalow for 20 years is a different case from someone buying a two-bedroom condo in the Pearl who expects to move within four.

Broadly, points tend to make more sense for long holding periods, stable payments, and buyers with cash beyond their reserve target. They tend to make less sense for short holds, tight cash, or anyone who expects to refinance.
Temporary Buydowns Are A Different Animal
A 2-1 buydown or 3-2-1 buydown is not the same as discount points, though the two get conflated constantly.
A temporary buydown places money into an escrow account that subsidizes your payment for the first year or two, then steps up to the note rate. The
note rate never changes
. You qualify at the note rate. When the subsidy runs out, your payment rises to what it was always going to be.

These are frequently paid for by a seller or builder as a concession. When someone else funds it, it can be a genuine benefit. Funding one with your own cash is a narrower call, because you are buying a short-term payment reduction rather than a permanent one.
The risk to name plainly: a temporary buydown is not a bet you can count on winning if your plan depends on refinancing before the subsidy expires. No one can promise where rates will be.
Where The Money Can Come From
You are not required to pay for points out of your own pocket.
Seller concessions
can cover points, subject to program limits based on loan type and down payment.
Builder incentives
on new construction in areas like Happy Valley or Hillsboro often take the form of rate buydowns through a preferred lender.
Lender credits
can offset other closing costs, freeing your cash for points, or the reverse.

If you are negotiating a purchase and the seller is willing to move on price or on concessions, run both. A price reduction lowers your loan amount and your property tax basis. A concession applied to a permanent buydown lowers your payment for as long as you hold the loan. Which is better depends on the numbers, and it is worth two minutes of arithmetic.
What To Do Next
Ask your loan officer for a pricing grid showing several rate and point combinations on the same loan, including at least one lender credit option.
Calculate breakeven in months for each. Write the number down.
Compare that to your honest expectation of how long the loan will last, not how long you will own the house.
Confirm that paying points does not dip into your post-closing reserves.
Check section A of your Loan Estimate to see exactly what you are being charged, and compare competing offers at matching rates.
If a seller concession is on the table, price a permanent buydown against a price reduction before deciding.
Points are neither a trick nor a bargain. They are a purchase, and the thing you are purchasing is time.

faqs.question: Is buying points worth it?
faqs.answer: It depends almost entirely on how long you keep the loan. Divide the cost of the points by the monthly principal-and-interest reduction to get a breakeven in months. If you expect to hold that specific loan comfortably longer than the breakeven, the math favors points. If you might sell or refinance before then, or the cash would drain your reserves, it usually does not.

faqs.question: How much does one point lower my rate?
faqs.answer: There is no fixed answer, because the tradeoff is set by daily market pricing and by your loan profile. The cost is predictable at 1 percent of the loan amount, but the rate reduction it buys changes with program, credit score, loan-to-value, and property type. The only reliable way to know is to ask for a current pricing grid showing several rate and point combinations side by side.

faqs.question: Can the seller pay for my points?
faqs.answer: Often yes, through seller concessions, subject to limits that vary by loan program and down payment. Builders on new construction frequently offer rate buydowns as an incentive as well. If a seller is willing to contribute, compare using that money for a permanent buydown against simply reducing the purchase price, since a lower price also lowers your loan amount and property tax basis.

faqs.question: What is the difference between points and a 2-1 buydown?
faqs.answer: Discount points permanently lower your note rate for the life of the loan. A 2-1 buydown temporarily subsidizes your payment for the first two years using escrowed funds, then your payment rises to the note rate, which never changed. You qualify at the full note rate either way. Temporary buydowns are most useful when a seller or builder is paying for them.

children.text: Most people evaluating a refinance are working from three scraps of information: a rate they saw in a headline, their current monthly payment, and a vague sense that their house is "worth more now." That's not enough to decide anything, and it's exactly enough to decide something badly.

A mortgage report — sometimes called a mortgage review, an equity analysis, or a refinance analysis depending on who's writing it — is the attempt to put everything relevant on one page. Not a quote. Not an application. A picture of where you actually stand.
Here's what belongs in one, how to read it, and what it can't tell you.
What a Mortgage Report Is

It's a written analysis of your current loan, your property's estimated value, your equity position, and a set of side-by-side scenarios showing what different refinance structures would do to your payment, your payoff date, and your total interest.
The important word is
side-by-side
. A quote gives you one option. A report gives you options next to each other, including the option of doing nothing — which is the comparison people most often skip and most often need.
It is not a commitment. Nothing in a report guarantees a rate, an approval, or an outcome. It's a decision-support document, and the honest ones say so.
The Six Things It Should Contain
1. Your current loan, in detail
Balance, rate, remaining term, loan type, whether you're paying mortgage insurance, and — critically — how much of your payment currently goes to principal versus interest.

That last item surprises people. Someone eight years into a 30-year loan is often still sending the majority of each payment to interest. Seeing that in print changes how you think about resetting the clock.
2. An estimated value and equity position
Usually an automated valuation drawing on recent comparable sales, sometimes supplemented by a real estate agent's opinion. It's an estimate, not an appraisal, and the report should say so.

In Portland this deserves scrutiny. Value can vary sharply within a few blocks — an unpermitted addition, a foundation on a slope in the West Hills, or a stretch of nonconforming lots can all pull a number away from the neighborhood average. Automated models don't see any of that.
Your equity position determines your
loan-to-value ratio
, which drives which programs you qualify for, whether mortgage insurance applies, and how much cash you could access.
3. Scenario comparisons
The heart of the document. A useful report shows at least three or four paths, each with payment, term, total interest, and closing costs.
On a
hypothetical
$350,000 balance at a
hypothetical 7%
with 25 years remaining, a report might lay out:
Do nothing
30-year at a
hypothetical 6%
— lowest payment, longest timeline
25-year at a hypothetical 6% — matches the current payoff date
15-year at a hypothetical 6% — highest payment, least total interest
Cash-out to a hypothetical 75% loan-to-value, if a funding need exists
Every scenario labeled hypothetical, because until you apply and are underwritten, that's what it is.
4. Closing cost detail

Broken into lender fees, third-party fees, government recording fees, and prepaids. Prepaids — taxes and insurance funding your escrow — should be separated out, because they're not a cost of refinancing. They're money you owe regardless.

Oregon's tax calendar makes this worth a look. Statements arrive in October with a discount for paying the full year by mid-November, so closing timing affects how much cash shows up on the settlement statement.
5. Breakeven analysis
Total costs divided by monthly savings. Any report that shows you a lower payment without showing you how long it takes to earn back the cost of getting it is doing half the job.
6. Credit and qualification context

Where your credit profile sits, what factors are affecting it, and whether anything in your file — a recent job change, a rental property, self-employment income — is likely to complicate underwriting. Better to know in advance.
What a Mortgage Report Is Not
It's not a Loan Estimate.

A Loan Estimate is a standardized three-page federal form issued after you apply on a specific property. It's binding in specific ways, with tolerance limits on certain fees. A mortgage report is informal and carries no such protections.
It's not an appraisal.
Value estimates in a report are educated approximations. The appraisal happens later and sometimes disagrees.
It's not a guarantee of anything.
Not a rate, not approval, not savings. Rates move daily and pricing depends on your final underwritten profile.
It's not individualized advice.

A report shows you numbers. What you do with them is a decision that should account for your full financial picture — and, depending on the situation, a conversation with a tax professional or attorney.
How to Actually Read One
Start with the "do nothing" column.
Everything else is measured against it. If it's not on the page, ask for it.
Compare total interest, not just payments.
A payment drop that extends your term by five years can cost more overall than it saves monthly.
Check the term on each scenario.
If every option is a 30-year, you're being shown one shape of loan.
Find the breakeven number.
Then ask yourself honestly how long you're keeping the house.
Verify the value estimate.
If it's meaningfully higher than what your street is actually selling for, every downstream number is optimistic.
Look for what's missing.
Escrow refunds from your old servicer, mortgage insurance removal, the three-day rescission period on a primary residence.
Special Situations Where a Report Earns Its Keep
Divorce.

When a property settlement is being negotiated, a report showing what's actually financeable — how much equity can realistically be accessed, whether one income supports the loan — prevents agreements that can't be executed. As a Certified Divorce Lending Professional, I see settlement language written around numbers nobody verified, and unwinding that later is expensive and slow.
Self-employment.
Qualifying income for a business owner is a calculation, not a number off a bank statement. Knowing what underwriting will actually count changes what's worth pursuing.
Multiple properties.
If you own a rental in Milwaukie alongside your primary residence, the interaction between them affects qualification in ways a single-loan view misses.
Mortgage insurance.

If you're paying it, a report should tell you whether your equity position now allows removal — sometimes without a refinance at all. That's a question worth asking before you spend thousands on closing costs to solve it the hard way.
What to Do Next
Gather three documents: your most recent mortgage statement, your homeowners insurance declaration page, and your latest property tax statement.
Write down what you're trying to accomplish. A report answering the wrong question is just tidy noise.
Request a review from a licensed loan officer and ask specifically for a
do-nothing baseline, total interest by scenario, and breakeven months
Sit with it for a few days. Nothing in a mortgage report expires so fast that you need to decide the afternoon you receive it.

Whether refinancing makes sense depends on current market conditions and the specifics of your loan and property. A good report doesn't decide for you — it just makes sure you're deciding with the whole picture in front of you.

faqs.question: Is a mortgage report the same thing as a loan estimate?
faqs.answer: No, they are different documents with different purposes. A mortgage report is an informal analysis showing your current loan, your equity, and several hypothetical scenarios side by side. A Loan Estimate is a standardized federal form issued after you apply on a specific property, with regulated fee tolerances. The report helps you decide whether to apply; the Loan Estimate documents what you applied for.

faqs.question: Does getting a mortgage report affect my credit?
faqs.answer: It depends on whether a credit report is pulled. Some reviews use only the information you provide and your property data, which has no credit impact at all. Others include a credit pull to assess qualification, which is a hard inquiry. Ask upfront which kind you are getting. A lender should tell you before pulling credit and obtain your authorization.

faqs.question: How accurate is the home value in one of these reports?
faqs.answer: Treat it as an estimate, not an appraisal. Most reports use automated valuation models built on recent comparable sales, which handle typical homes in uniform neighborhoods reasonably well. They struggle with unusual properties, unpermitted work, and steep or irregular lots, all of which are common around Portland. The appraisal during underwriting is what actually determines your loan-to-value ratio.

faqs.question: What should I bring to a mortgage review?
faqs.answer: Three documents cover most of it: your most recent mortgage statement, your homeowners insurance declaration page, and your latest property tax statement. Add recent pay stubs or tax returns if you want the qualification portion to be meaningful. Most useful of all is a clear sentence about what you are trying to accomplish, since that determines which scenarios are worth modeling.
