children.text: There are people in Portland with $90,000 in savings, a decade at the same employer, and no credit score at all. Not a bad score. No score. They paid cash for cars, never carried a credit card, and the bureaus have nothing recent enough to score.
They get told they are unbankable. That is wrong. What they are is unscoreable by an automated system, which is a different problem with a different solution.

The solution is called manual underwriting, and it has existed for as long as mortgages have. A human being reviews your file, looks at how you have actually handled obligations, and makes a decision. It is slower and more document-heavy. It is not exotic.
No Score Is Not The Same As A Bad Score
This distinction matters more than anything else in this article, so it goes first.
A
low score
means the bureaus have data and the data is unflattering. Late payments, collections, high utilization, a recent bankruptcy. Underwriting sees documented evidence of repayment problems.
No score
means insufficient data. Common reasons include:
Never opening credit accounts by choice or by religious conviction
Recent immigration to the United States, with credit history that does not transfer
Young borrowers with no accounts yet
Older borrowers who paid everything off years ago and let accounts close
Divorce that left one spouse without accounts in their own name

Underwriters treat these very differently. A borrower with no score and a clean 24-month rent and utility history is not viewed as a risky borrower. They are viewed as an unmeasured one. The job is to measure them another way.

Worth naming here: opening a credit card three months before applying does not create a usable score fast enough for most timelines, and it can complicate the file. If you are 12 months or more out from buying, building traditional credit is reasonable. If you are 60 days out, manual underwriting is the more practical path.
What Actually Counts As Credit
The underwriting term is
nontraditional credit references
or alternative credit. The idea is simple: prove you pay things on time using accounts that do not report to the bureaus.
Most programs want to see a set of these, typically covering at least 12 months, with the housing payment carrying the most weight:
Rent history.
The single most important reference. Twelve months of cancelled checks, bank statements showing consistent transfers, or a verification of rent completed by a property management company.
Utilities.
Electric, gas, water, sewer, trash, in your name.
Insurance.
Auto, renters, health, life. Premiums paid directly, not deducted from a paycheck.
Phone and internet.
Landline, mobile, cable.
Childcare or tuition.
Regular documented payments.
Medical payment plans, storage units, gym memberships.
Anything recurring with a paper trail.

The quality standard is documentation. A landlord who is a relative, or rent paid in cash with no records, will not clear underwriting. Rent paid by bank transfer to a management company for two years is close to ideal.

Start pulling these records early. Utility companies will produce payment histories on request, but not always quickly, and reconstructing a year of cash-app rent transfers the week before closing is a miserable exercise.
Which Loan Programs Allow This
Not every program permits manual underwriting with nontraditional credit, and the flexibility varies.
FHA

is the most common path. FHA has established guidelines for manually underwritten files with nontraditional credit, including specific expectations around housing payment history, debt ratios, and reserves. Individual lenders may apply stricter overlays on top of the agency rules.
VA

loans can be manually underwritten for eligible veterans and service members. VA underwriting places heavy weight on residual income, which is the money left over each month after the mortgage, debts, taxes, and estimated maintenance. For a borrower with no score but strong cash flow, this can be a favorable framework.
USDA
allows manual underwriting for eligible rural properties, with its own documentation standards and income limits. Geography controls eligibility here.
Conventional

loans do permit some borrowers without credit scores through the automated underwriting systems, but the requirements are tighter, and they generally lean toward primary residences with meaningful reserves and documented alternative credit.

A practical note for mixed households: if one spouse has a strong score and the other has none, you may have the option of applying with one borrower only, or of running both scenarios. Using only the scored borrower means only that person's income counts, which can shrink the qualifying amount. It is worth pricing both ways rather than assuming.
What Underwriters Look At Instead
When the score disappears, the rest of the file gets more scrutiny. Expect attention on:
Housing payment history.
Twelve months clean is the baseline expectation. Any late rent payment in that window is a real problem.
Debt-to-income ratio.
Manual underwriting typically applies tighter DTI limits than automated approvals, and exceeding them requires documented compensating factors.
Cash reserves.
Months of mortgage payments remaining after closing. This is often the strongest compensating factor a no-score borrower has.
Payment shock.
The jump from your current rent to the proposed housing payment. A borrower going from $1,600 rent to a $3,400 payment will get questions. One going from $2,400 to $2,700 will not.
Employment stability.
Two years in the same field, documented.
Down payment sourcing.

Cash that has been sitting in a bank account is easy. Cash accumulated at home and deposited recently is difficult, because underwriters cannot verify where it came from. If you keep money outside the banking system, deposit it and let it season for several months before applying.
Oregon Specifics Worth Knowing
The
Oregon Bond Residential Loan Program

, administered through Oregon Housing and Community Services, is layered on top of a standard first mortgage, most often FHA, VA, USDA, or conventional. It offers options structured around either a rate benefit or cash assistance toward down payment and closing costs, subject to income limits, purchase price limits, and first-time buyer rules that vary by county.

Because it sits on top of an underlying program, the underlying program's credit rules apply. If you can get to an FHA manual approval, the Oregon Bond overlay is worth asking about. Income and price limits differ between Multnomah, Washington, and Clackamas counties and the rest of the state, so the county line can genuinely change your eligibility.

The other Oregon reality is price point. Manual underwriting rewards modest payments relative to income. In the Portland metro, that often means looking at outer neighborhoods, condos, or communities like Gresham, Oregon City, or Forest Grove rather than close-in inner east side. That is not a consolation prize. It is how the math works for a lot of first purchases.
What To Do Next
Pull your credit through a lender rather than a consumer app. Confirm whether you truly have no score or a thin file with a usable score. These lead to different paths.
Gather 12 to 24 months of rent documentation now. Bank statements, cancelled checks, or a landlord verification form.
Build a list of three to four other recurring accounts in your name and request payment histories.
Move any cash savings into a bank account and leave it alone for several months.
Do not open new credit accounts in the 90 days before applying without talking to your loan officer first.
Ask specifically whether the lender does manual underwriting in house. Some do not, and finding that out at week three is expensive in time.
A thin credit file lengthens the process. It does not end it.

faqs.question: Can I actually buy a house if I have never had a credit card?
faqs.answer: Yes, through manual underwriting, which evaluates your payment history using nontraditional references instead of a score. You will need documented proof that you pay recurring obligations on time, usually 12 months or more of rent plus utilities, insurance, or similar accounts. FHA and VA loans are the most common routes. Expect more paperwork and a longer timeline than a scored borrower would face.

faqs.question: Should I open a credit card just to get a score before I apply?
faqs.answer: Only if you are at least a year away from buying. Scores generally need several months of history on new accounts before they become usable, and a brand new account opened right before application can complicate underwriting. If your purchase is months away rather than a year, gathering alternative credit documentation is usually the faster path. Talk to a loan officer before opening anything.

faqs.question: What if my spouse has good credit and I have none?
faqs.answer: You have options, and they should be priced both ways. Applying with only the scored spouse simplifies underwriting but removes the other person's income from qualifying, which usually lowers the loan amount. Applying jointly means the file goes manual. Which one produces a better result depends on how much income the unscored spouse contributes and how strong the documented alternative credit is.

faqs.question: Does paying rent on time actually help me get approved?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is the most heavily weighted alternative credit reference in a manually underwritten file. Underwriters want to see 12 consecutive months with no late payments, verified through bank statements, cancelled checks, or a verification form from a management company. Rent paid in cash to an individual landlord is much harder to document, so switching to a traceable payment method well before you apply is worthwhile.

children.text: A homeowner once told me she refinanced because her rate dropped by a full point, and she was thrilled about it right up until she added the numbers a year later and realized she'd committed to paying about $19,000 more in interest than if she'd done nothing.
She got a lower rate. She got a lower payment. She still lost.

The math behind that is not exotic, and it's the reason "is refinancing worth it" can't be answered with a rate comparison. Whether a refinance makes sense depends on where the market sits at the moment you're looking, what your existing loan actually is, and how long you'll keep the house. What follows is a framework that stays true regardless of what rates do.
Rule One: A Lower Rate Is Not the Goal
The rate is an input, not an outcome. What you actually care about is one of these:
Lower monthly payment, because cash flow is tight right now
Less total interest paid over the life of the debt
A specific dollar amount of cash for a specific purpose
A structural change — dropping mortgage insurance, converting from adjustable to fixed, removing a borrower

Those goals conflict with each other. Optimizing for the lowest monthly payment usually means paying more interest overall. Optimizing for total interest usually means a higher monthly payment. You have to pick.
If you don't pick, the loan picks for you, and it tends to pick the one that looks best on a payment comparison sheet.
Rule Two: Do the Breakeven Division
This is the single most useful calculation in refinancing, and it takes ten seconds.
Total closing costs ÷ monthly payment savings = months to breakeven.
Work through a hypothetical. A borrower has a
hypothetical
remaining balance of $350,000 at a
hypothetical 7%
rate with 25 years left. Principal and interest run about
$2,474/month
They refinance into a
hypothetical 6%
30-year loan on the same balance. New payment: about
$2,098/month
. Savings:
$376/month
Closing costs: a
hypothetical $6,000
about 16 months
If they keep the house more than 16 months, they're ahead on cash flow. If they sell in a year, they paid $6,000 to save roughly $4,500.

The Portland-area wrinkle: people move more than they plan to. If a job change, a growing family, or a move from inner Southeast out to Hillsboro is plausible in the next two years, weight that heavily. Breakeven assumes you stay.
Rule Three: Monthly Savings and Total Interest Are Different Questions
Back to that same hypothetical borrower. They saved $376 a month. Here's what happened to their total interest.
Staying put:
$2,474 × 300 remaining months = $742,200 total, of which about
$392,200 is interest
Refinancing to a 30-year:
$2,098 × 360 months = $755,280 total, of which about
$405,280 is interest
— plus $6,000 in costs, so call it
A lower rate, a lower payment, and roughly
paid overall. That's the trap. They didn't get a worse rate. They got five extra years of it.
Rule Four: Amortization Resets, and That's the Hidden Cost
Every mortgage front-loads interest. In year one, most of your payment services interest and very little touches principal. By year twenty, that ratio has flipped.
When you refinance into a fresh 30-year term, you go back to year one of that curve. You've been grinding your way up the hill, and you slide back down to the bottom with a slightly gentler slope.
This is not an argument against refinancing. It's an argument against refinancing into a full new 30-year term by default, which is what happens when nobody asks for anything else.
Two ways around it:
Match your remaining term
Same hypothetical borrower, but into a
25-year
loan at a hypothetical 6% instead of 30. Payment: about
. Savings: about
$219/month
— smaller, less exciting.
Total interest over the 25 years: about
, plus $6,000 costs. Compared to the $392,200 of doing nothing, that's roughly
$59,700 saved
instead of $19,000 lost.
Same rate. Same house. Different answer, entirely because of term.
Take the 30-year and keep paying the old amount
Take the lower payment for flexibility, then voluntarily pay the old $2,474 anyway. On that hypothetical 30-year at 6%, paying $2,474/month retires the loan in roughly
20.5 years
instead of 30, with total interest around

You get the lower required payment as a safety valve and the faster payoff as a habit. The catch is that it depends entirely on you actually doing it, every month, for two decades. Be honest about whether you're that person.
Rule Five: Understand What You're Paying and How
Closing costs come in a few flavors and they're not interchangeable.
Lender fees
— origination, underwriting, processing.
Third-party fees
— appraisal, title insurance, escrow, credit report.
Government fees
— county recording. Multnomah, Washington, and Clackamas counties each set their own schedules.
Prepaids
— property taxes and insurance funding your new escrow account. These aren't a cost of the refinance; they're money you'd owe regardless. Don't let them inflate your breakeven math.

Oregon's property tax calendar matters here. Statements go out in October and there's a discount for paying the full year by mid-November, so where your closing falls in that cycle can meaningfully change the cash you bring to the table.
You can also pay
points
— money upfront to lower the rate — or take a
lender credit
, a higher rate in exchange for the lender covering costs. Points make sense over long holding periods. Credits make sense over short ones. Both are just trades between now-money and later-money.
Rule Six: Some Reasons Don't Need Breakeven Math
A few refinances are worth doing even when the cash math is only neutral:
Removing an ex-spouse from a mortgage after a divorce, so their credit and borrowing capacity are freed and yours is clearly defined
Eliminating mortgage insurance you can't otherwise cancel
Escaping an adjustable rate when uncertainty itself is the problem
Consolidating a high-rate second mortgage or HELOC into one fixed obligation
In these cases you're buying a structural outcome, not a payment. Price it honestly, but don't judge it purely on breakeven.
Rule Seven: Count the Costs You Can't See on a Quote
Two things routinely get left out of the comparison.
The first is
time already served

. If you're eleven years into a 30-year loan, you've absorbed the interest-heavy stretch of the amortization schedule. That's a sunk investment in a very literal sense, and starting over hands a chunk of it back. Quotes never show this line item, because it isn't a fee.
The second is
the cost of doing this again

. Some borrowers refinance every couple of years chasing improvements, paying a new set of closing costs each time and never advancing far into any amortization schedule. Each individual transaction can look reasonable on its own breakeven sheet while the cumulative pattern is expensive.
Neither is a reason to avoid refinancing. They're reasons to treat it as a decision with a lifespan rather than a transaction you optimize in isolation.
What to Do Next
Pull your mortgage statement. Write down
balance, rate, remaining term, and whether you pay mortgage insurance
. Every calculation starts here.
Name your goal in one sentence, and notice whether it's a cash-flow goal or a total-cost goal.
Get a
Loan Estimate
— the standardized federal form — from more than one lender, and compare page 2 line by line rather than comparing rates.
Run the breakeven division yourself. Then ask for the same quote at a term matching your remaining years and compare total interest, not just payments.
Ask directly: "What does this cost me over the life of the loan versus doing nothing?" A good loan officer will have that number ready.
Whether a refinance is worth it today depends on conditions today and on the specific loan sitting on your specific house. The framework doesn't expire. The answer does.

faqs.question: How much does my rate need to drop to make refinancing worth it?
faqs.answer: There is no universal threshold, despite the old rules of thumb. The right test is breakeven: divide total closing costs by your monthly savings to get the number of months required to recover the cost. A large loan balance can justify a small rate improvement, while a small balance may not justify a large one. Loan size matters as much as rate.

faqs.question: Is it worth refinancing if I'm going to move in a couple of years?
faqs.answer: Often not, because you may sell before recovering the closing costs. Run the breakeven division and compare it honestly to your expected time in the home. If breakeven lands at eighteen months and you expect to be in the house four years, the math works. If you might relocate next spring, the costs likely outrun the savings.

faqs.question: Why did my total interest go up even though my rate went down?
faqs.answer: Because you probably restarted the amortization clock. Refinancing from twenty-two remaining years into a fresh thirty-year term adds eight years of payments, and that added time can outweigh the savings from a lower rate. Ask for a quote at a term matching your remaining years, then compare total interest rather than just the monthly payment.

faqs.question: Should I roll the closing costs into the loan or pay them upfront?
faqs.answer: It depends on how long you plan to keep the loan. Rolling costs in preserves cash but means paying interest on those costs for the loan's life. Paying upfront costs more today and less overall. If you expect to keep the loan a long time, paying upfront usually costs less; over a short horizon, keeping your cash often makes more sense.

children.text: Three buyers, all looking around $475,000 in the Portland area. One has a 640 credit score and 4 percent saved. One is an Army veteran with almost no cash but steady income. One works remotely and is open to living 40 minutes outside the metro.

Those three people should almost certainly use three different loan programs. Not because one program is superior, but because FHA, VA, and USDA were each built to solve a specific problem, and the problems do not overlap much.
This article assumes you already know roughly what each program is. What follows is the sorting logic: which one fits which situation, what each one costs you, and when each is the wrong choice.
Start With Three Questions
Before comparing features, answer these. They eliminate most of the confusion.
Have you or your spouse served?
If yes, VA is almost always the first program to price. Everything else is a comparison against it.
Where is the property, exactly?
USDA eligibility is determined by mapped location, not by how rural a place feels. Address-level check, every time.
What is your credit profile and how much cash do you have?
This decides whether FHA is solving a real problem or creating an unnecessary cost.
The order matters. Eligibility comes before preference. There is no point falling in love with USDA financing on a house in Beaverton.
FHA: The Credit Flexibility Program
FHA exists to make financing available to borrowers whose credit or debt profile makes conventional underwriting difficult.
What it does well:
Lower minimum credit score thresholds than most conventional programs
More tolerance for higher debt-to-income ratios, especially with compensating factors
Allows manual underwriting, including for borrowers with thin or nontraditional credit
Shorter waiting periods after bankruptcy or foreclosure than conventional guidelines
Gift funds and down payment assistance layer on relatively easily
What it costs:
An upfront mortgage insurance premium, typically financed into the loan
An annual mortgage insurance premium paid monthly, which on most low down payment FHA loans
remains for the life of the loan
Property condition standards that can complicate offers on older or deferred-maintenance homes
When FHA is the wrong choice:

if you have a solid credit score and 5 percent or more down. In that case conventional financing with cancellable private mortgage insurance is often the cheaper long-run structure, because the insurance goes away. FHA also struggles in competitive multiple-offer situations where listing agents assume appraisal and condition friction, and it is a poor fit for a fixer that will not pass minimum property requirements.
VA: Hard To Beat On Structure, If You Are Eligible
For eligible veterans, active duty service members, National Guard and Reserve members, and certain surviving spouses, the VA program is structurally different from everything else.
What it does well:
No down payment requirement for most eligible borrowers with full entitlement
No monthly mortgage insurance
, which is the single biggest structural advantage in the government lineup
Underwriting built around residual income, which can accommodate borrowers whose ratios look tight on paper
Limits on certain fees the veteran can be charged
The loan can be assumable by a qualified buyer, which matters more in some rate environments than others
What it costs:
A one-time VA funding fee, which varies by down payment amount, service category, and whether it is a first or subsequent use. Veterans receiving VA disability compensation are generally exempt.
Property standards through the VA appraisal process
Entitlement is a finite resource if you already have a VA loan outstanding
When VA is the wrong choice:

rarely, but it happens. If you are buying a property type VA does not permit, or if you have limited remaining entitlement and a conventional loan preserves it for a future purchase, the comparison is worth running. Some veterans with substantial down payments and strong credit find conventional competitive once the funding fee is factored in. And in a fast market, a seller weighing offers may treat the appraisal process as a variable, which is a negotiation issue rather than a loan issue.
USDA: Geography First, Everything Else Second
USDA Guaranteed loans offer no-down-payment financing for eligible properties in designated areas, with household income limits.
What it does well:
No down payment for qualified borrowers
Guarantee fees that are often lower than FHA mortgage insurance, though structures differ
Works well for buyers with modest income who are open to living outside the urban core
What it costs:
Household income limits
, based on everyone in the household, not just borrowers. Two solid incomes can disqualify you.

Geographic restriction. Much of the dense Portland metro is not eligible. Areas farther out in Columbia, Yamhill, Clackamas, Marion, and Polk counties may include eligible tracts, but maps get updated and you must check the specific address on the USDA eligibility site.
Primary residence only, and property standards apply
When USDA is the wrong choice:

when your income is near the limit and rising, when you need to close fast, or when the commute math does not survive contact with reality. A no-down-payment loan on a house 50 minutes from your job in Northwest Portland is not free if you are driving it five days a week.
Head To Head, By Situation
Veteran with little cash:
VA, then compare against FHA only if something disqualifies the VA loan.
640 score, 3.5 percent down, metro property:
FHA, with a plan to refinance into conventional once credit and equity improve.
720 score, 5 percent down:
price conventional first. FHA may cost more over time because of the permanent mortgage insurance.
Moderate income, willing to buy in an eligible outlying area:
check USDA before anything else, since it is the only one with a hard geographic gate.
Self-employed with strong reserves but complicated tax returns:
the program matters less than the documentation approach. All three can work.
Thin or no credit score:
FHA and VA both allow manual underwriting with nontraditional credit references.
What Nobody Mentions Until Underwriting
All three are primary residence programs.
None of them finance a vacation home or a pure investment purchase. Multi-unit properties can work if you occupy one unit.
Property condition matters more than with conventional.

Peeling paint on a pre-1978 home, a failing roof, or an unpermitted addition can stall an FHA or VA file. In Portland, where a lot of the housing stock predates World War II, this comes up constantly.
Oregon Bond can layer on top.

The Oregon Bond Residential Loan Program can pair with FHA, VA, USDA, or conventional first mortgages, offering either a rate benefit or cash assistance, subject to income limits, purchase price limits, and first-time buyer rules that vary by county. Multnomah, Washington, and Clackamas counties have different thresholds than much of the rest of the state, so where you buy affects what you qualify for.
Refinancing later is part of the plan, not an admission of failure.
FHA borrowers commonly move to conventional financing once equity and credit support it, specifically to shed mortgage insurance.
A Decision Framework
Confirm VA eligibility. If eligible, price VA first.
Check the exact property address on the USDA eligibility map and check household income against the applicable limit.
Pull credit and get an accurate score, not an app estimate.
If your score and down payment support conventional financing, price conventional against FHA on total cost over five and ten years, not just the monthly payment.
Factor property condition. An older home with deferred maintenance may narrow your options regardless of what you qualify for.
Ask whether Oregon Bond or another down payment assistance program can sit on top of whichever first mortgage you choose.
What To Do Next

Get a Certificate of Eligibility if you are a veteran. Check the USDA map for any address you are seriously considering. Then ask a loan officer to run side-by-side scenarios on the same property and price point, showing upfront cost, monthly payment, and total mortgage insurance or guarantee cost over a realistic holding period.
The program that wins on the monthly payment is not always the one that wins over ten years. Look at both columns before you decide.

faqs.question: Which government loan is easiest to qualify for?
faqs.answer: FHA generally has the most flexible credit and debt-to-income standards, which makes it the common landing spot for borrowers with lower scores or past credit events. VA underwriting can be more accommodating for eligible veterans because it emphasizes residual income, but eligibility is limited to those who served. USDA has moderate credit flexibility but adds hard geographic and household income limits that disqualify many metro buyers.

faqs.question: Can I use a USDA loan in the Portland area?
faqs.answer: Not in most of the dense metro, since USDA eligibility is set by mapped areas that exclude urban zones. Some communities farther out in counties like Columbia, Yamhill, Marion, and Polk may include eligible tracts, and portions of outer Clackamas County sometimes qualify. Maps change, so check the specific property address on the USDA eligibility site before writing an offer.

faqs.question: If I qualify for a VA loan, is there ever a reason not to use it?
faqs.answer: Occasionally. If you have limited remaining entitlement from an existing VA loan and want to preserve it for a future purchase, or if you have a large down payment and strong credit where conventional financing compares well after the funding fee, running both scenarios makes sense. Property type restrictions can also rule it out. For most eligible buyers with limited cash, VA is still the first option to price.

faqs.question: Does FHA mortgage insurance really last forever?
faqs.answer: On most FHA loans with a minimum down payment, the annual mortgage insurance premium stays for the life of the loan, so it does not cancel through equity growth the way conventional PMI does. The usual exit is refinancing into a conventional loan once your credit and equity support it. That is a normal, planned step rather than a failure, and it is worth mapping out before you choose FHA.

title: Adjustable-Rate Mortgages Versus Fixed-Rate Mortgages: What's Right for You?
excerpt: If you have ever wanted to understand better the adjustable-rate vs fixed-rate decision.

seo.metaDescription: If you have ever wanted to understand better the adjustable-rate vs fixed-rate decision.

children.text: Two buyers make an offer on the same house in Beaverton. One takes a 30-year fixed. The other takes a 7/6 ARM. Five years later, one of them has moved to Denver and the other is still in the kitchen arguing about backsplash tile.
The one who moved probably made the better financing choice — and it had nothing to do with predicting interest rates. It had to do with how long they were going to own the house.

That is the whole decision, more or less. Everything else is mechanics. But the mechanics matter, because an ARM you do not understand is a genuinely bad idea, and an ARM you do understand is sometimes the obviously correct one.
The Basic Difference
A
fixed-rate mortgage

has one interest rate for the entire loan term. Your principal and interest payment on day one is identical to your principal and interest payment in year 28. Property taxes and insurance can still move, so your total payment may change, but the loan portion does not.
An
adjustable-rate mortgage

has a fixed rate for an initial period, then adjusts periodically for the remaining term. A 7/6 ARM is fixed for seven years, then adjusts every six months. A 5/6 ARM is fixed for five, then every six months. A 10/1 ARM is fixed for ten, then annually.
Note that the loan term is still 30 years in almost every case. "7/6 ARM" does not mean a seven-year loan. It means a 30-year loan whose rate stops being fixed after seven years.
How an ARM Rate Is Actually Calculated
After the initial fixed period ends, your rate is not set by your lender's mood. It is set by a formula:
Index + Margin = Fully Indexed Rate
The
index

is a published, market-driven benchmark. Most modern ARMs use SOFR (Secured Overnight Financing Rate), typically a 30-day average. It moves with the market and neither you nor your lender controls it.
The
margin
is a fixed number added on top, set at origination and written into your note. It does not change for the life of the loan.
So if a hypothetical index sits at 4% and your margin is 2.75%, your fully indexed rate would be 6.75% — subject to caps.

The margin is the part you should actually scrutinize when comparing ARM offers, because it is the permanent component. A lower teaser rate with a higher margin can be worse over time than the reverse.
Caps: The Part That Makes ARMs Survivable
Caps limit how much your rate can move. They are usually written as three numbers, like
or
Initial cap
— the maximum the rate can change at the very first adjustment.
Periodic cap
— the maximum change at each subsequent adjustment.
Lifetime cap
— the maximum the rate can ever be above your starting rate.

A 5/1/5 structure on a hypothetical 6% start rate means: the first adjustment can take it no higher than 11%, each subsequent adjustment can move it no more than 1 percentage point, and it can never exceed 11% at any point in the loan.
Many ARMs also have a
floor
— a rate below which they will not drop, regardless of the index.
The Stress Test You Should Actually Run
Here is the single most useful exercise for anyone considering an ARM, and it takes about ten minutes.
Calculate your payment at the lifetime cap.
Not the index-plus-margin projection. Not a "rates will probably come down" assumption. The worst legally permitted outcome under your note.

On a hypothetical $400,000 loan at a hypothetical 6% start rate with a 5/1/5 cap structure, you would calculate the principal and interest payment at 11% on the remaining balance after the fixed period. Then look at that number and ask one question:
If I still owned this house and that was my payment, would I be fine?

If the answer is yes, the ARM is a reasonable instrument for you. If the answer is "well, I'd probably have sold by then" — that is not a yes. That is a plan that depends on a future you cannot control. Job changes, family changes, and market conditions all have opinions about when you sell.
If the answer is genuinely yes, you are in the right place. And if the answer is no, take the fixed rate and stop thinking about it.
When a Fixed Rate Makes Sense
The fixed-rate mortgage is the default for good reason, and it is the right answer for most people buying a primary residence they intend to keep.
Fixed makes sense when:
You plan to stay long-term.
If your ownership horizon is longer than the ARM's fixed period, you are accepting adjustment risk for a benefit you'll only enjoy for part of the time.
Your income is fixed or tightly budgeted.
Retirees, single-income households, and anyone on a strict budget benefit enormously from a payment that does not move.
You don't want to think about it.
This is a legitimate reason. There is real value in a decision you never have to revisit.
The rate spread between fixed and ARM is narrow.
ARMs compensate you for taking on risk. When that compensation is small, you are taking risk for very little in return.
When an ARM Makes Sense

ARMs get a bad reputation from the pre-2008 era, and some of it was earned — but the loans that caused that damage were structurally different from today's ARMs. Negative amortization, no-documentation underwriting, and payment-option structures are largely gone. Modern ARMs are fully amortizing and underwritten to the same ability-to-repay standards as fixed loans.
An ARM may make sense when:
You have a known, short ownership horizon.
Medical residents, military families with orders, and people on defined corporate assignments often know they are leaving. Paying for 30 years of rate certainty you'll use for four is expensive.
You expect substantially higher income.
Someone finishing a residency or heading into a partnership track has a different risk profile than someone whose income is flat.
You plan to pay the loan down aggressively.
If a chunk of the balance disappears before the first adjustment, the adjustment applies to a much smaller number.
The spread is wide enough to matter.
When the ARM's initial rate is meaningfully lower, the savings during the fixed period can be real. Just count them honestly, after tax, over the period you'll actually hold the loan.
Portland-Specific Considerations

Portland's employment base skews toward sectors with real mobility — technology, healthcare, athletic apparel and footwear. Corporate relocations and role changes are common enough that "how long will I own this" is a genuinely open question for a lot of buyers here.
If you're using the
Oregon Bond Residential Loan Program
, note that its offerings are structured around fixed-rate loans, so the ARM question generally doesn't arise there.

And one more thing worth saying: an ARM does not commit you to holding the ARM. You can refinance out of it. But treat that as a possibility, not a plan. Refinancing depends on your credit, your income, your home's value, and market conditions at that future date — none of which anyone can promise you today.
What to Do Next
Write down your honest ownership horizon
before you look at any rate. Five years? Twenty? "No idea" is a real answer, and it points toward fixed.
Ask for the full ARM disclosure
on any ARM you're considering — index, margin, all three caps, floor, and adjustment frequency.
Run the lifetime-cap payment
and react to that number, not the start rate.
Compare the ARM and fixed side by side
over your actual holding period, not over 30 years.
If you want help building that comparison for your specific scenario, that's a real conversation. This article is general education — your numbers deserve an actual look.

faqs.question: Can my ARM payment really double?
faqs.answer: Not under modern cap structures, but it can rise substantially. Your lifetime cap defines the ceiling — commonly five percentage points above your start rate. On a hypothetical $400,000 loan, moving from a hypothetical 6% to a capped 11% is a large payment increase, though not a doubling. Calculate that exact number before signing anything.

faqs.question: What happens to my ARM if I still own the house in year 25?
faqs.answer: It keeps adjusting on schedule until the loan is paid off, typically at year 30. There's no point where an ARM converts back to fixed on its own. If you're still in the home well past the fixed period, your options are to keep riding the adjustments, refinance if you qualify at that time, or pay the balance down.

faqs.question: Is an ARM cheaper than a fixed-rate mortgage?
faqs.answer: During the initial fixed period, ARMs typically carry a lower starting rate than comparable fixed loans — that's the compensation for taking on adjustment risk. Whether it's cheaper overall depends entirely on how long you keep the loan and what the index does after the fixed period ends. Nobody can tell you that in advance.

faqs.question: How do I know which index my ARM uses?
faqs.answer: It's stated in your note and in the ARM disclosure you receive during the application process. Most ARMs originated in recent years use a 30-day average SOFR. Ask your loan officer directly for the index name, the margin, and all three caps in writing before you lock — those four numbers define the entire loan.

title: What Is a Mortgage Refinance, In Plain English
excerpt: Are you faced with the opportunity to refinance your home?

seo.metaDescription: Are you faced with the opportunity to refinance your home?

children.text: Imagine you borrowed $20 from your brother at a bad interest rate, and then your sister offered to lend you $20 at a better one. You'd take your sister's $20, hand it to your brother, and now you owe your sister instead.
That's a refinance. Everything else is paperwork.

The reason it feels complicated is that mortgages involve title companies, escrow accounts, appraisals, and a stack of disclosures thick enough to prop open a door. But the transaction underneath is genuinely that simple:
new loan pays off old loan, you owe the new lender now.
Let's walk through one from start to finish.
The Setup
Meet a hypothetical homeowner. Call her Dana. She bought a house in Southeast Portland five years ago.
Here are her
hypothetical
numbers — invented for illustration, not quotes, not current market figures:
Original loan:
Original rate: a
hypothetical 7%
fixed
Original term: 30 years
Payment (principal and interest): about
$2,661/month
Remaining balance after 5 years: roughly
Remaining term: 25 years
Dana has heard she should look at refinancing. She wants to know what that actually involves.
Step One: Something Changes
A refinance only makes sense if something has changed since you got your original loan. Usually one of these:
Market rates have moved
Your credit profile has improved
Your home's value has gone up, changing your loan-to-value ratio
Your goals have changed — you want a shorter term, or a lower payment, or one name on the loan instead of two
You've been paying mortgage insurance and now have enough equity to drop it
If nothing has changed, there's nothing to gain. That's not a sales-resistant attitude, it's just arithmetic.
For Dana, let's say she's exploring whether a
hypothetical 6%
rate would be worth pursuing. That's an illustrative number chosen to make the math legible — not a rate available to anyone, including Dana, who is fictional.
Step Two: Application and Underwriting
Dana applies. This part looks a lot like buying a house, minus the house hunting.
She provides:
Income documentation — pay stubs, W-2s, tax returns if self-employed
Asset statements, to show she can cover closing costs
Authorization for a credit pull
Her current mortgage statement and homeowners insurance policy
Underwriting reviews all of it. They're answering one question: does this borrower, at this income, with this credit, against this property, represent an acceptable risk on this new loan?
Approval is never guaranteed for anyone. Underwriting is a real review, not a formality, and refinances get declined.
Step Three: The Appraisal
The lender needs to know what the house is worth, because the loan amount can only be a certain percentage of the value.

Sometimes an automated valuation is accepted and no appraiser visits. Sometimes a full appraisal is required. In the Portland metro, where a 1920s Craftsman in Ladd's Addition and a 2005 build in Happy Valley are wildly different products, appraisers lean heavily on nearby comparable sales — which is why values can shift block to block.
Say Dana's home appraises at a
hypothetical $520,000
. Against her $376,000 balance, that's a loan-to-value of about 72%. Comfortable territory for most conventional programs.
Step Four: The Costs
This is the part people skip, and it's the part that decides everything.
Dana's
hypothetical
closing costs:
Lender origination and underwriting: $1,800
Appraisal: $700
Title insurance and escrow fees: $1,900
County recording fees: $200
Prepaid interest and escrow funding: varies
Call it roughly
in fees, ignoring prepaids, which aren't really a cost — they're money you'd owe anyway, just paid on a different schedule.
She has three ways to handle that $4,600:
Pay it in cash
at closing
Roll it into the loan
, borrowing $380,600 instead of $376,000
Take a lender credit
, accepting a slightly higher rate in exchange for the lender covering some costs
None of these is free. Option two means paying interest on your closing costs for up to 30 years. Option three means paying more every month forever in exchange for paying less once.
Step Five: Does the Math Work?
Here's the whole decision in one comparison.
Dana's current loan:
$376,000 remaining at a hypothetical 7%, 25 years left. Payment about
New loan option A — 30-year at a hypothetical 6%:
$380,600 (costs rolled in). Payment about
Monthly difference: roughly
$379 less
per month.
That looks great. But notice what happened to the timeline. Dana had 25 years left. She just signed up for 30. She saves $379 a month and adds five years of payments.
New loan option B — 25-year at a hypothetical 6%:
$380,600 over 25 years. Payment about
Monthly difference: roughly
$209 less
per month, and she keeps her original payoff date.
Option A wins on cash flow. Option B wins on total interest paid. Which one is "better" depends entirely on what Dana actually needs — and there's no universal answer.
Step Six: Breakeven
If Dana pays her $4,600 in cash instead of rolling it in, the question becomes: how long until the monthly savings pay back the cost?
At a hypothetical $209/month savings on the 25-year option:
$4,600 ÷ $209 = about 22 months.

If Dana plans to stay in the house well beyond two years, that math is favorable. If she's thinking about relocating to Bend in eighteen months, she'd spend $4,600 to save about $3,760 and then leave. That's not a refinance, that's a donation.
Breakeven is the single most useful number in this entire conversation. Ask for it every time.
Step Seven: Closing
Assuming everything checks out, Dana signs at escrow. Then a few things happen that surprise first-time refinancers:
A three-day right of rescission.
On a primary residence, federal law gives you three business days after signing to cancel. The loan doesn't fund until that window closes.
You skip a payment — sort of.
Because mortgage interest is paid in arrears, the timing usually means one month with no payment due. That's not a gift. The interest is accounted for in the payoff.
Your old escrow account gets refunded.
Your prior servicer mails you the balance, usually within a few weeks. Meanwhile you're funding a new escrow account at closing. Don't spend the refund before it arrives.
Your loan may be sold.
The servicer who collects your payment can change. The terms of your note cannot.
What to Do Next
Find your current mortgage statement and write down your balance, rate, and remaining term. You cannot evaluate a refinance without these.
Decide what you're actually optimizing for: lower monthly payment, faster payoff, cash for a purpose, or a name removed from the loan.
Ask any lender you talk to for a
Loan Estimate
. It's a standardized federal form, which means you can lay two of them side by side and actually compare.
Do the breakeven division. Total costs divided by monthly savings. If the answer is longer than you plan to own the home, the rest of the details don't matter.
A refinance isn't complicated. It's just consequential — which is a different thing, and a better reason to slow down.

faqs.question: Do I get money back when I refinance?
faqs.answer: Only if you do a cash-out refinance. A standard rate-and-term refinance simply replaces your loan balance, so nothing meaningful comes back to you at closing. You may receive an escrow refund from your prior servicer a few weeks later, but that is your own money being returned, not proceeds. Plan around it arriving late rather than counting on it at signing.

faqs.question: Why do I skip a payment when I refinance?
faqs.answer: You are not actually skipping anything. Mortgage interest is paid in arrears, meaning your payment covers the month that just ended. Because of that timing, the payoff of your old loan and the start of your new one usually leave one calendar month without a payment due. The interest for that period is included in the payoff figure, so nothing is forgiven.

faqs.question: Can I change my mind after I sign?
faqs.answer: Yes, on a primary residence you generally have three business days to cancel. Federal law provides a right of rescission on refinances of an owner-occupied home, and the loan does not fund until that window closes. You have to deliver the cancellation notice in writing within the deadline. The right does not apply to investment properties or second homes.

faqs.question: How long does a refinance take from start to finish?
faqs.answer: Typically several weeks, though it varies with lender volume, appraisal scheduling, and how quickly you return documents. The steps are application, underwriting, appraisal or appraisal waiver, title work, closing, and the rescission period. Delays most often come from missing paperwork, so gathering income and asset documents before you apply is the single most effective thing you can do.

excerpt: Have you been told that PMI is always bad? The truth is more nuanced.

seo.metaDescription: Have you been told that PMI is always bad? The truth is more nuanced.

children.text: Here is a conversation I have had more times than I can count. A buyer has about 12 percent saved for a house in Beaverton. She wants to push her purchase out two years so she can hit 20 percent and avoid private mortgage insurance. She has a number in her head for what PMI costs, and that number came from somewhere on the internet.
She has never priced her actual PMI. She has also never priced two more years of rent, two more years of whatever home prices do, and two more years of not owning the asset.

PMI is not a penalty. It is not a scam. It is a fee you pay so that someone else takes a risk you cannot cover with cash. Sometimes that trade is smart. Sometimes it is not. It depends entirely on the numbers in front of you, which is an unsatisfying answer that happens to be the true one.
What PMI Actually Does
Private mortgage insurance protects the lender, not you. If you default and the property sells for less than the loan balance, the insurer covers part of that loss. That is the whole product.

Because the lender is protected, it will lend to you at a loan-to-value ratio above 80 percent. Without mortgage insurance, that loan largely does not exist in the conventional market. So the honest framing is not PMI versus no PMI. It is PMI versus not buying yet.

PMI pricing is driven by a handful of inputs: your loan-to-value ratio, your credit score, your debt-to-income ratio, whether the loan is fixed or adjustable, and whether the property is a primary residence. Rates vary by insurer and change over time, so anyone quoting you a single universal number is guessing.

The general shape is predictable, though. The more you put down and the stronger your credit profile, the less it costs. A borrower putting 15 percent down with excellent credit is in a very different pricing tier than a borrower putting 3 percent down with a mid-600s score. Those two people should not be making the same decision.
One more distinction that trips people up:
PMI is a conventional loan product

. FHA loans have their own mortgage insurance, called MIP, with different rules, different pricing, and importantly, different cancellation terms. VA loans have no monthly mortgage insurance at all, just a one-time funding fee for most borrowers. When someone tells you mortgage insurance is forever, they are usually thinking about FHA.
The Four Ways To Pay For It
Most buyers assume PMI means one thing: a monthly add-on. There are actually several structures, and loan officers do not always volunteer all of them.
Monthly borrower-paid PMI.
The default. A monthly premium added to your payment, cancellable later. Lowest upfront cost, highest cost if you keep it for years.
Single-premium PMI.

You pay a lump sum at closing, or roll it into the loan, and there is no monthly premium. This can work well when a seller credit or lender credit is covering closing costs, because it converts someone else's money into a permanently lower payment. The catch: if you sell or refinance in two years, that premium is largely spent, and some single premiums are non-refundable.
Lender-paid PMI.
The lender pays the premium and charges you a higher interest rate instead. There is no separate PMI line item, which people love. But it is baked into the rate for the life of the loan and
does not cancel
when you hit 20 percent equity. To get rid of it, you refinance.
Split premium.
A smaller upfront amount plus a reduced monthly. Less common, occasionally the cheapest total.

There is also the piggyback structure, where a second mortgage covers part of the down payment so the first stays at 80 percent LTV. It still exists, but the second lien usually carries a higher rate and is often adjustable, so it needs to be compared honestly rather than assumed to be clever.
The Math Nobody Runs
Here is the comparison that actually settles it, using clearly hypothetical numbers.
Say a hypothetical buyer is looking at a $500,000 home in the Portland metro. Option A: put 10 percent down now and carry PMI. Option B: keep renting for 24 months to reach 20 percent down.
To compare them, you need four figures:
The actual PMI premium quoted for your credit profile and LTV, not an internet average
How many months you are likely to carry it before cancellation
Your monthly rent during the waiting period
What you give up or gain by owning versus not owning over that stretch

If a hypothetical PMI premium is a small fraction of what you pay in rent each month, waiting two years to avoid roughly 30 to 60 months of a modest premium is not obviously the winning move. If your premium quote is high because of a thin credit file, the answer may flip.
The point is that PMI is a cost, and costs get compared to other costs. It does not get compared to zero, because zero is not on the menu unless you have the cash.
How PMI Ends, And Why That Matters More Than The Price
On conventional loans, borrower-paid PMI is cancellable. That single fact reframes the whole product, because it turns a permanent expense into a temporary one.
Under the federal Homeowners Protection Act, for a primary residence:
You can
request cancellation
once the balance reaches 80 percent of the original value, if you are current and the loan has seasoned appropriately
The servicer must
automatically terminate
it at 78 percent of original value based on the amortization schedule
There is a final backstop at the midpoint of the loan term
Separately, most servicers will consider cancellation based on a
new appraised value

rather than the original purchase price, subject to their own seasoning requirements and equity thresholds. In neighborhoods where values have moved or where you have done real renovation work, this is the path people forget about. It costs an appraisal fee and a phone call.

FHA is the contrast case. For most FHA loans with a low down payment, the annual MIP stays for the life of the loan, and the way out is a refinance into a conventional loan once you have equity. That is not a reason to avoid FHA. It is a reason to know what you signed up for and to revisit it later.
When PMI Really Is A Bad Deal
Being fair to the villain narrative, there are situations where paying it is a poor trade:
Your quote is priced off a weak credit file.
Spending three months fixing reporting errors or paying down revolving balances can move you into a better tier, and the premium difference compounds monthly.
You are stretching to the edge of your budget.
If the premium is the thing that makes the payment work, the payment does not work.
You are choosing lender-paid PMI on a loan you expect to hold for decades.
No cancellation means no exit without a refinance.
You are 1 or 2 percent away from 20 percent
and the cash is sitting in a checking account doing nothing. Closing that gap is usually the easy call.
What does not belong on that list is the general belief that PMI is money thrown away. So is rent. So is interest. The question is what each dollar buys.
What To Do Next
Ask for an actual PMI quote based on your credit score, down payment, and loan type, not a rule of thumb.
Ask your loan officer to price monthly, single-premium, and lender-paid side by side on the same loan scenario so you can see total cost over three, five, and ten years.
Estimate how long you would realistically carry it, factoring in extra principal payments if you plan to make them.
Compare that to the full cost of waiting, including rent.
If you already own and have gained equity, call your servicer and ask what their cancellation requirements are. Put a reminder on your calendar to check annually.
PMI is a tool with a price tag. Price it, use it if it helps, and cancel it when you can.

faqs.question: How long am I stuck paying PMI?
faqs.answer: On a conventional loan, until you reach the equity thresholds set by federal law or your servicer, which is often several years rather than the life of the loan. You can request cancellation at 80 percent of original value, and automatic termination happens at 78 percent. Many servicers also allow cancellation based on a new appraisal. FHA mortgage insurance follows different rules and often lasts the life of the loan.

faqs.question: Is it dumb to buy a house with less than 20 percent down?
faqs.answer: No, it is a tradeoff, and for a lot of Portland-area buyers it is a reasonable one. Putting less down means mortgage insurance and a larger loan balance, but it also means you keep cash reserves and stop paying rent sooner. The right answer depends on your PMI quote, your rent, your reserves, and how long you plan to stay.

faqs.question: Can I get rid of PMI without refinancing?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, if you have borrower-paid monthly PMI on a conventional loan. You reach the required equity level through payments, appreciation, or improvements, then ask your servicer about their cancellation process, which may involve a new appraisal. Lender-paid PMI is the exception. Because it is built into the interest rate, removing it generally requires a refinance.

faqs.question: Does PMI protect me if I lose my job?
faqs.answer: No. Private mortgage insurance protects the lender against loss if the loan defaults, not you. If you want protection against income loss, that is a separate conversation about emergency savings, disability coverage, or mortgage protection life insurance. Keeping three to six months of expenses liquid after closing does more for your household risk than any insurance line item on the loan.

title: Using Government Home Loans for Your Next Purchase: Everything You Need to Know
excerpt: The housing market was blazing for more than two years, and government programs can help.

seo.metaDescription: The housing market was blazing for more than two years, and government programs can help.

children.text: A veteran buying in Gresham writes an offer with zero down. The listing agent tells the seller that VA loans are slow and the appraisals kill deals. The offer gets passed over for a conventional buyer with 10% down.

That scenario happens regularly, and it is built almost entirely on outdated assumptions. Government-backed loans are not a lesser tier of financing. They are underwritten by the same lenders, closed on the same timelines, and in some cases carry terms conventional financing cannot match.
Here is how they actually work, what they cost, and where the real friction points are.
What "Government-Backed" Actually Means
The federal government is not lending you money. Your lender is.

What the government does is insure or back the loan, which reduces the lender's downside risk. That reduced risk is what allows lower down payments, more flexible credit standards, and sometimes better pricing than the borrower's profile would otherwise support.
In exchange, these loans come with rules — property condition standards, occupancy requirements, insurance fees, and program-specific limits. The rules are the price of the access.
FHA Loans
Insured by the Federal Housing Administration, FHA is the workhorse program for buyers with thinner credit files or higher debt loads.
Core features:
3.5% down
with a qualifying credit score; higher down payment required below that threshold.
More flexible debt-to-income allowances
than most conventional programs.
Assumable
in many cases, meaning a future buyer may be able to take over the loan under its existing terms if they qualify.
County-based loan limits.
The Portland metro counties — Multnomah, Washington, Clackamas — share a higher limit than most rural Oregon counties, reflecting local price levels. Limits are set annually.
The cost structure has two parts. An
upfront mortgage insurance premium
is financed into the loan, and an
annual MIP

is paid monthly. The important detail: at less than 10% down, that annual premium generally stays for the life of the loan. Many FHA borrowers eventually refinance into conventional financing once they have enough equity to drop it.

For borrowers with strong credit, a low-down-payment conventional loan with cancellable PMI often ends up cheaper over time. For borrowers with credit challenges, FHA frequently wins. It is a side-by-side comparison, not a default.
VA Loans
Backed by the Department of Veterans Affairs and available to eligible veterans, active-duty service members, National Guard and Reserve members, and certain surviving spouses.
The terms are genuinely strong:
No down payment required
with full entitlement.
No monthly mortgage insurance
, which is the feature that most changes the monthly math.
No loan limit
for borrowers with full entitlement, though lender overlays apply.
Limits on certain closing costs
the borrower can pay.
The main cost is the
VA funding fee

, a one-time charge that varies by down payment, service category, and whether it is a first or subsequent use. It can be financed into the loan. Borrowers receiving VA compensation for a service-connected disability are typically exempt, along with certain surviving spouses — an exemption that gets missed more often than it should.

On the appraisal side, VA appraisals include minimum property requirements. This is where the reputation comes from. In practice, most issues are resolvable and most VA transactions close on ordinary timelines.
USDA Loans
The least known of the three, and the one people wrongly assume does not apply near Portland.
USDA Rural Development loans offer
no down payment
for eligible borrowers buying in eligible areas. Eligibility runs on two tracks:
Property location.

Determined by a USDA-maintained map, checked by address. Boundaries are broader than most people assume — portions of Yamhill, Columbia, Clackamas, and outer-metro areas can fall within eligible zones. Maps get updated, so verify current eligibility rather than relying on old information.
Household income.
Limits are based on total household income and household size for the county, and they include income from household members who are not on the loan.
Costs include an upfront fee that can be financed and a smaller annual fee paid monthly, both generally lower than comparable FHA mortgage insurance.
For buyers willing to look toward Scappoose, Newberg, or St. Helens rather than inner Portland, USDA can be the difference between buying now and waiting.
The Oregon Bond Layer
Worth knowing: the
Oregon Bond Residential Loan Program
through Oregon Housing and Community Services is a state program, not a federal one, and it can pair with FHA, VA, USDA, or conventional financing.

It offers either a reduced interest rate or cash assistance toward down payment and closing costs, subject to income and purchase price limits that vary by county. Eligibility generally targets buyers who have not owned a primary residence in the past three years, with exceptions in certain targeted areas. Only participating lenders can originate it.
Stacking Oregon Bond with a government loan is where some of the most workable Portland-area financing structures come from.
Property Condition: The Real Friction Point
All three federal programs require the property to meet condition standards. This is the legitimate source of the reputation government loans carry.
Common items appraisers flag:
Peeling or chipping paint on homes built before 1978, due to lead-based paint rules.
Missing handrails on stairs, or exposed wiring.
Roof condition and remaining useful life.
Non-functioning heat sources, plumbing, or electrical systems.
Well and septic testing where applicable, particularly on USDA properties.

Portland's older housing stock — the pre-1940 bungalows and foursquares across inner Southeast and North Portland — encounters these more often than newer construction in Washington County. It is manageable when everyone knows what to expect. It becomes a problem when it surfaces two weeks before closing.
The fix is front-loading. Have your agent flag likely condition issues before the offer, and negotiate repairs or credits with the appraisal standards in mind.
Does a Government Loan Weaken My Offer?
It can affect how an offer is perceived, which is a different thing than actual risk. Listing agents who have had a bad experience years ago carry that forward.
Things that help:
A
fully underwritten preapproval
rather than a prequalification letter.
A
realistic closing timeline
you can actually hit.
A lender whose name the listing agent recognizes and who will pick up the phone.
Sensible terms elsewhere in the offer — inspection approach, possession, earnest money.
A well-documented VA buyer is not a weaker counterparty than a conventional buyer. Making that legible to the other side is part of the job.
What To Do Next
Check eligibility first.
For VA, request your Certificate of Eligibility. For USDA, check the property map and income limits by county.
Ask for a side-by-side comparison
of the government option against a low-down-payment conventional loan, including total monthly cost and long-run insurance expense.
Verify the FHA loan limit
for the specific county you are shopping in.
Ask about Oregon Bond eligibility
and whether it can layer with your program.
Talk with your agent about property condition
before writing on an older home.

Bri Lindley, Mortgage Loan Officer with The Lindley Team at Movement Mortgage (NMLS #1367416), works with Portland-area buyers using FHA, VA, USDA, and Oregon Bond financing. This is general education, not individualized advice or an offer of credit.

faqs.question: Can I really buy a house with no money down in Oregon?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you qualify for a VA or USDA loan. VA loans require no down payment for eligible veterans, service members, and certain surviving spouses with full entitlement. USDA loans require no down payment for eligible borrowers buying in eligible areas, subject to household income limits. You would still need funds for closing costs, though those can sometimes be covered by seller credits or assistance programs.

faqs.question: Are there USDA eligible areas near Portland?
faqs.answer: Yes. USDA eligibility boundaries extend into parts of the outer Portland metro, including areas of Columbia, Yamhill, and Clackamas counties. Eligibility is determined address by address on a USDA-maintained map that gets updated periodically, so check the current map for any specific property rather than assuming based on how developed an area looks.

faqs.question: Do sellers avoid FHA and VA offers?
faqs.answer: Some listing agents are wary, usually based on old experiences with appraisal condition requirements. In practice, government loans close on ordinary timelines with the same lenders as conventional financing. A fully underwritten preapproval, a realistic closing date, and a lender who communicates with the listing agent do more to strengthen your position than the loan type does to weaken it.

faqs.question: What's the catch with FHA mortgage insurance?
faqs.answer: With less than 10% down, FHA annual mortgage insurance generally stays for the life of the loan rather than cancelling at 80% equity the way conventional PMI does. There is also an upfront premium financed into the balance. That does not make FHA a bad choice, but it does mean borrowers with strong credit should compare it against a low-down-payment conventional loan before deciding.

title: What Is Interest Rate Volatility? Your Guide
excerpt: If you're looking to purchase your first home, you're probably watching interest rates closely.

seo.metaDescription: If you're looking to purchase your first home, you're probably watching interest rates closely.

children.text: A borrower gets a quote on a Tuesday morning. They think about it over lunch, call back at 2 p.m., and the number has moved. Nobody did anything shady. The bond market repriced mid-session, and the lender reissued rate sheets.

That is volatility, and it is the single most misunderstood feature of mortgage pricing. It is also the thing that should shape how you think about locking, about timing, and about whether a fixed or adjustable rate fits your situation.
What Volatility Means in Mortgage Terms
Volatility is the size and frequency of price movement, not the direction. A market can be volatile while trending down, trending up, or going nowhere.
In calm periods, mortgage rate sheets might hold steady for days. In volatile periods, lenders can issue a
mid-day reprice
— sometimes more than one — because the underlying securities moved enough to make the morning's pricing unprofitable.

This matters because a mortgage quote is not like a price tag on a shelf. It is a live market quote with a short shelf life. Understanding that changes how you behave: you stop treating a rate sheet as a promise and start treating a lock as the actual decision point.
Why Mortgage Rates Move At All
Mortgage rates are set by the market for
mortgage-backed securities
. Investors buy bundles of home loans and accept a yield in return. When investors demand more yield, rates rise. When they accept less, rates fall.

What drives that demand is mostly expectations about inflation and economic growth. Fixed payments 20 years out are worth less if inflation runs hot, so inflation surprises tend to move mortgage rates quickly.

The economic calendar is therefore the volatility calendar. Inflation reports, the monthly employment report, Federal Reserve meetings and the commentary afterward, Treasury auctions, and occasionally a geopolitical event — these are the days when rates can move more in a morning than they did the previous two weeks.

A point worth repeating: the Fed does not set mortgage rates. Fed decisions influence expectations, and expectations move the bond market. That indirect chain is why mortgage rates sometimes move opposite to what a Fed announcement would suggest, which annoys everyone equally.
How Volatility Shows Up in Your Actual Loan
The practical touchpoints are these.
Rate locks.

A lock commits the lender to specific pricing for a set number of days — commonly 30, 45, or 60. Longer locks generally cost more because the lender carries the risk longer. If your closing slips past the lock expiration, an
extension fee
typically applies.
Float-down provisions.
Some lenders offer a one-time option to capture a better rate if the market improves after you lock. Terms, costs, and thresholds vary, and availability is not universal.
Floating.
Choosing not to lock means you accept whatever pricing exists when you eventually do. That can work out in your favor or against it. Nobody can predict which.
Repricing during your process.

If you are floating and the market moves against you between preapproval and offer acceptance, your qualifying numbers can shift. This is why it is worth knowing what payment you are comfortable with, not just what you are approved for.
Long timelines.

New construction in areas like Hillsboro, Happy Valley, or Ridgefield can involve closing dates months out. Extended lock programs exist for this, sometimes with an upfront fee. Ask early, not at framing inspection.
Fixed-Rate: Paying for Certainty

A fixed-rate mortgage locks the interest rate for the full term. Your principal and interest does not change. Taxes and insurance still move, so your total payment can drift, but the loan portion is settled.

What you are buying is insulation from volatility. What you pay for it is a starting rate that is typically higher than the initial rate on a comparable adjustable-rate loan, because the lender is absorbing decades of uncertainty on your behalf.
For most owner-occupied buyers planning to stay put, the certainty is worth it. Predictability has real value when it is your housing payment.
Adjustable-Rate: Trading Certainty for a Lower Start
An ARM has a fixed introductory period, then adjusts on a set schedule. A 7/6 ARM is fixed for seven years, then adjusts every six months.
After the fixed period, the rate is calculated as an
index plus a margin

. The index — commonly SOFR-based on current loan products — moves with the market. The margin is a fixed number set at origination and disclosed in your note. Add them, apply the caps, and that is your new rate.
Caps
are the guardrails and the part borrowers should read most carefully:
Initial cap:
how much the rate can move at the first adjustment.
Periodic cap:
how much it can move at each subsequent adjustment.
Lifetime cap:
the maximum the rate can ever reach above the start rate.
Here is the stress test worth running. On a
hypothetical $400,000 loan starting at a hypothetical 5.5%

, principal and interest would be about $2,271. If the lifetime cap allowed the rate to reach a hypothetical 10.5%, principal and interest on the remaining balance would land substantially higher — well over $3,000 per month.
That is a worst case, not a forecast. But if that number would break your budget, the ARM is not the right product regardless of how attractive the starting rate looks.
How To Actually Decide
Three questions do most of the work.
How long will you realistically hold this loan?
If your honest answer is under the fixed period of the ARM with room to spare, the adjustable structure deserves consideration. If you are unsure, that uncertainty argues for fixed.
Can you absorb the capped worst case?
Not the expected case — the capped maximum. If yes, you have genuine flexibility. If no, the question is settled.
What is the actual spread between the two?

Sometimes the gap between fixed and adjustable pricing is wide enough to justify the risk. Sometimes it is narrow enough that the certainty is nearly free. This changes with market conditions, so it is a question to ask at the moment you are deciding, not a rule to memorize.

Refinancing is often mentioned as the escape hatch from an ARM adjustment. It sometimes is. But refinancing depends on future rates, future home values, and your future credit and income — none of which anyone can promise.
What To Do Next
Ask your loan officer to price fixed and adjustable side by side
, with the full cap structure and margin disclosed for the ARM.
Calculate your capped worst-case payment
and check it against your actual budget.
Confirm your lock period matches your contract timeline
, plus a buffer for appraisal and underwriting.
Ask whether a float-down is available
and what it costs.
Know your walk-away payment
— the number above which the deal stops making sense for you — before the market moves.

Bri Lindley, Mortgage Loan Officer with The Lindley Team at Movement Mortgage (NMLS #1367416), can walk through fixed and adjustable scenarios for your specific timeline. All figures above are hypothetical illustrations for education, not quotes or offers of credit.

faqs.question: Why do mortgage rates change every day?
faqs.answer: Mortgage rates are priced off the mortgage-backed securities market, which trades continuously. When investor demand shifts — usually because of inflation data, employment reports, Federal Reserve commentary, or Treasury supply — pricing moves, and lenders update their rate sheets accordingly. On especially active days, a lender may reprice more than once before markets close.

faqs.question: Should I lock my rate or float it?
faqs.answer: Locking removes uncertainty for a set number of days; floating keeps you exposed to market movement in both directions. There is no way to know in advance which will work out better, so most borrowers lock once they have an accepted offer and a firm closing timeline. If your closing date is far out, ask about extended lock options and whether a float-down provision is available.

faqs.question: When does an adjustable-rate mortgage actually make sense?
faqs.answer: An ARM can make sense when your expected time in the loan is comfortably shorter than the fixed introductory period and you could still absorb the payment if the rate hit its lifetime cap. Run that capped worst-case number before deciding. If it would strain your budget, or if your timeline is uncertain, the predictability of a fixed rate is usually the better fit.

faqs.question: What happens to my payment when my ARM adjusts?
faqs.answer: At adjustment, your rate is recalculated as the loan's index plus its fixed margin, then limited by the initial, periodic, and lifetime caps disclosed in your note. Your payment is then recalculated on the remaining balance over the remaining term. Your rate can go down as well as up, but plan around the capped maximum rather than an assumption about market direction.
