title: Before You Put a 20 Percent Down Payment On a House: Read this
excerpt: Are you planning on putting down 20% of the full purchase price?

seo.metaDescription: Are you planning on putting down 20% of the full purchase price?

children.text: A couple sits down with $145,000 saved and a $650,000 house under contract in the Portland metro. Twenty percent is $130,000. Writing that check leaves them with $15,000, minus closing costs, minus moving, minus the washer and dryer the sellers are taking with them.

They are about to become homeowners with roughly one month of expenses in the bank, in a house built in 1948, in a region where the rainy season lasts about seven months and finds every flaw in a roof.
Nobody in that transaction is doing anything wrong. But the question they never got asked is the important one: what is that last $50,000 of down payment actually buying, and what is it giving up?
What The Extra Cash Actually Buys
Moving from 10 percent down to 20 percent down does three things, and it is worth being precise about each.
It eliminates private mortgage insurance
on a conventional loan. Real money, though on most conventional loans it is a temporary cost that cancels once you reach the equity thresholds.
It reduces the loan balance
, which lowers your principal and interest payment proportionally.
It may improve loan pricing
, since loan-to-value is an input to rate and fee adjustments.

Notice what is not on that list. It does not increase your net worth. Moving $50,000 from a savings account into home equity is a transfer between two assets you already own. Your balance sheet is unchanged the moment the transaction closes.
What changes is the
form
of the asset. Cash is liquid, low-yielding, and available at 2 a.m. Home equity is illiquid, does not spend, and requires a bank's permission and several weeks to access.

The closest thing to a return on that extra down payment dollar is the interest you avoid paying on it, which is roughly your note rate. That is not nothing. But it is a return you cannot withdraw, cannot redeploy, and cannot use in an emergency.
The Liquidity Problem
Here is the uncomfortable structural fact about home equity. It is easiest to access when you least need it and hardest to access when you most need it.

Lose your job and you cannot pull equity out, because underwriting requires income. Have a medical event and get behind on payments, and cash-out refinancing becomes difficult. Values dip in your neighborhood and your equity cushion shrinks on paper, tightening your options further.
Meanwhile, the dollars you kept in a savings account do not ask about your employment status.

This is why the phrase house rich, cash poor exists as a description of a problem rather than an achievement. A homeowner with a small mortgage balance and $2,000 in the bank is in a more fragile position than one with a larger balance and $40,000 in reserves, even though the first one looks better on a spreadsheet.
Reserves Come First
Before optimizing the down payment, fund the boring things. In rough priority order:
Three to six months of total housing costs and living expenses
, liquid. More if your income is variable, commission-based, or self-employed.
A home maintenance fund.

Portland's housing stock skews old. Cast iron sewer laterals, knob and tube wiring, seismic retrofitting on unreinforced foundations, moss-friendly roofs, and basements that have opinions about February. A single sewer line replacement can run into five figures.
Closing costs and moving costs
, which are not the down payment and routinely get underestimated.
The first-year furnishing and fixing budget.
Everyone spends it. Almost nobody plans it.
Only after those are covered does the marginal down payment dollar deserve consideration.

One practical note: lenders count reserves as a positive underwriting factor. Draining your accounts to hit 20 percent can weaken your file in other ways, particularly for self-employed borrowers or those with tighter debt ratios. Occasionally, putting less down produces a stronger overall application.
What Else That Money Could Do
This is where honest comparison lives. The extra down payment dollar is competing against other uses, and some of them are strong.
Employer retirement match.
If you are not capturing a full match because cash is tight, that is generally the first place a dollar should go.
High-interest debt.
Credit card balances at rates well above any mortgage rate are a clear comparison. Paying those down also lowers your debt-to-income ratio, which can help you qualify.
Immediate, necessary home work.
Money spent on a failing roof or an electrical panel is not optional spending. It is deferred cost you inherited.
Income stability.
For self-employed borrowers or households with one income, cash reserves are the functional equivalent of insurance.
Long-term investing.

This one is genuinely uncertain. Market returns are not promised, and comparing an uncertain return to a certain interest cost is a personal risk tolerance question, not a math question. Anyone who tells you the answer is obvious is selling something.
Notice that most of these are not exotic. They are ordinary financial housekeeping that gets skipped because 20 percent has cultural weight.
Getting The Money Back Out Is Not Free
Suppose you put the full 20 percent down and two years later need $40,000 for a remodel or a family situation. Your options:
Cash-out refinance.
New closing costs, new appraisal, new rate on the entire balance, which may be higher or lower than your current one. Nobody can promise which.
Home equity line of credit.
Usually a variable rate, subject to underwriting, and lenders can reduce or freeze lines under some conditions.
Sell.
Transaction costs of several percent of the sale price.
Each path costs time, money, and approval. The cash you kept in a savings account costs a transfer.
That asymmetry is the entire opportunity cost argument compressed into one paragraph. Converting liquid cash into equity is easy and cheap. Converting equity back into cash is slow and expensive.
When A Big Down Payment Genuinely Is Right
The case for putting down 20 percent or more is real in several situations, and it deserves equal airtime.
You have ample reserves already.
If the 20 percent comes out of surplus rather than out of your emergency fund, most of this article does not apply to you.
You are crossing a loan limit.
Putting more down to stay within conforming loan limits, which vary by county and are higher in some Portland-area counties than in others, can meaningfully change your loan terms.
Your PMI quote is expensive.
Pricing varies by credit profile. If yours came back high, avoiding it is worth more.
You want the lowest possible fixed payment
because you are approaching retirement, expect income to decline, or simply value a smaller monthly obligation over flexibility.
You are competing on an offer
and a stronger down payment materially improves how a seller views your financing.
Cash keeps you up at night.
Sleep is a legitimate input. If a smaller balance lets you stop thinking about the mortgage, that is worth something real, even if it does not show up in a spreadsheet.
The Middle Path Most People Miss
The choice is not 5 percent or 20 percent. Down payments are a dial, not a switch.

A borrower can put 12 or 15 percent down, keep a real emergency fund, carry a smaller mortgage insurance premium than they would at 5 percent, and cancel that premium later once equity thresholds are reached. That is often the structurally sensible compromise, and it almost never gets discussed because it lacks a round number.
If you are a first-time buyer, it is also worth asking whether the
Oregon Bond Residential Loan Program

applies. It pairs with FHA, VA, USDA, or conventional first mortgages and offers options built around either a rate benefit or cash assistance toward down payment and closing costs, subject to income limits, purchase price limits, and first-time buyer rules that differ between Multnomah, Washington, and Clackamas counties and other parts of Oregon. Programs like this can change the calculus entirely.
What To Do Next
Write down your total cash, then subtract closing costs, moving costs, and a maintenance buffer. That remainder is what is actually available for a down payment.
Set your reserve target first, in months of full housing cost plus living expenses. Protect it.
Ask your loan officer to price the same purchase at three down payment levels, showing payment, mortgage insurance cost, and cash remaining after closing for each.
Ask what the mortgage insurance cancellation path looks like at each level.
Check whether your county's conforming loan limit creates a threshold worth targeting.
If you are a first-time buyer, ask about Oregon Bond and other down payment assistance before you commit the cash.
Twenty percent is a fine answer. It just needs to be an answer you chose, not a number you inherited.

faqs.question: Is it bad to put down 20 percent if it wipes out my savings?
faqs.answer: It is risky, yes. Closing with almost no cash means any early repair, income disruption, or unexpected expense has to go on a credit card or wait. Home equity is not accessible in an emergency without a refinance or a line of credit, both of which require income and underwriting. Most buyers are better served protecting three to six months of expenses first, then deciding on the down payment with what remains.

faqs.question: Does a bigger down payment actually make me wealthier?
faqs.answer: Not at the moment you make it. Moving cash into home equity is a transfer between two assets you already own, so your net worth is unchanged on closing day. What changes is liquidity. You reduce future interest cost, which is a genuine benefit, but you trade spendable money for money that requires a loan or a sale to access. Both sides of that trade are real.

faqs.question: What is the right down payment if it is not 20 percent?
faqs.answer: There is no universal number, but a common sensible landing spot is whatever amount lets you keep a full emergency fund intact. For many buyers that ends up somewhere between 10 and 15 percent, which reduces mortgage insurance costs compared to a minimum down payment while preserving liquidity. Ask for the same purchase priced at three levels and compare cash remaining after closing, not just payment.

faqs.question: When does putting 20 percent down really make sense?
faqs.answer: When the money comes out of surplus rather than your safety net. It also makes sense when a larger down payment keeps you within a county conforming loan limit, when your mortgage insurance quote came back expensive due to credit profile, when you are prioritizing the smallest possible fixed payment heading into retirement, or when a stronger down payment improves your position in a competitive offer situation.

title: Before You Put a 20 Percent Down Payment On a House: Read this
excerpt: According to reports, 2 in 5 people think that 20% down is required.

seo.metaDescription: According to reports, 2 in 5 people think that 20% down is required.

children.text: Here is what that misconception costs in real terms. On a hypothetical $550,000 home in the Portland metro, a 20% down payment is $110,000. A 5% down payment is $27,500.

For most households, the gap between those two numbers is not a budgeting exercise. It is several years of waiting, during which they are paying someone else's mortgage and betting that home prices and rates cooperate.
That does not mean 20% down is wrong. It means it is a choice with real tradeoffs on both sides, and it deserves to be treated as one.
Where the 20 Percent Rule Came From
The number is not arbitrary. Conventional lenders require mortgage insurance when a loan exceeds 80% of the property's value, so 20% down is the threshold where PMI disappears.
That is it. That is the entire origin. It is a lending guideline that got repeated until it became folk wisdom, then got repeated some more until people started believing it was a legal requirement.
It is not. Conventional loans go to 3% down for qualified first-time buyers and 5% for many others. FHA goes to 3.5%. VA and USDA go to zero for eligible borrowers.
What 20 Percent Actually Buys You
When it makes sense, it makes real sense. Putting 20% down gets you:
No monthly mortgage insurance.
The most direct benefit.
A smaller loan
, which means less interest paid over the life of the loan and a lower payment.
Better rate pricing in some scenarios
, since loan-to-value is one of the inputs lenders price on.
More cushion against a value decline
, which matters if you might need to sell in a short window.
A cleaner-looking offer
in the eyes of some listing agents, though this is more perception than substance.

That last point gets oversold. Sellers care about whether the deal closes. A well-documented buyer with 5% down and a fully underwritten preapproval is a stronger counterparty than someone with 20% down and a thin prequalification letter.
What It Costs You
The expenses that show up after closing are the ones people underestimate.

A Portland bungalow from the 1920s will need something. Sewer line, knob-and-tube, a roof, a furnace, foundation work — pick one. Draining your savings to reach a round number and then discovering the sewer scope came back bad is a genuinely bad month.
There is also
reserve requirements
. Many loan programs want to see a certain number of months of payments in the bank after closing. Emptying accounts to hit 20% can, ironically, weaken your file.

And there is timing. Every year spent saving is a year of rent, a year of not building equity, and a year of exposure to whatever the market does. That exposure runs both directions — prices can soften — but you are making a bet either way.
The Real Minimums
Worth knowing what the actual floor is by program:
Conventional:
3% down for qualifying first-time buyers, 5% for many repeat buyers. PMI applies below 20%, and it is cancellable.
FHA:
3.5% down with a qualifying credit score. More flexible on credit and debt ratios, but mortgage insurance typically stays for the life of the loan at that down payment.
VA:
No down payment required for eligible veterans, service members, and certain surviving spouses. No monthly mortgage insurance. A one-time funding fee applies, with exemptions for some borrowers.
USDA:
No down payment for eligible borrowers in eligible rural areas. Income limits apply. Parts of the outer Portland metro fall inside eligible boundaries — the map is address-specific and changes.
Jumbo:
Varies by lender and loan size; typically requires more down than conforming loans.
Oregon-Specific Programs Worth Knowing
The
Oregon Bond Residential Loan Program
, run through Oregon Housing and Community Services, is the one most Portland-area buyers have never heard of.

It offers two structures. One reduces the interest rate below what the borrower might otherwise obtain. The other provides cash assistance calculated as a percentage of the loan amount, which can go toward down payment and closing costs, in exchange for a slightly higher rate.

Eligibility is based on household income limits and purchase price limits that vary by county, and the program is generally aimed at buyers who have not owned a primary residence in the past three years — with exceptions in certain targeted areas. It can be layered with conventional, FHA, VA, or USDA financing, and only participating lenders can originate it.

There are also local options. The Portland Housing Bureau and various county and nonprofit programs periodically offer down payment assistance, though funding availability and terms change. Anyone shopping in Washington County versus Multnomah County should check both, since program footprints do not always line up with where people are actually looking.
The Middle Path Most People Skip
The conversation tends to get framed as 3% versus 20%, which is a false binary. Ten percent down is a real option and frequently the sweet spot.

At 10%, PMI factors drop meaningfully compared to 5% down, the loan is smaller, and you keep a substantial chunk of cash. On the hypothetical $550,000 purchase, that is $55,000 down instead of $110,000 — half the cash, most of the benefit.

There is also a timing argument for putting less down now. PMI is cancellable on conventional loans once you reach 80% equity. So a buyer at 10% down is not signing up for a permanent expense; they are signing up for a temporary one with a defined exit.

Buying with less down and keeping reserves also preserves optionality. Cash in the bank can become a principal reduction later. A larger down payment cannot become cash again without a refinance or a sale.
What To Do Next
Price out three scenarios
— 5%, 10%, and 20% down — on the same target price, with total monthly payment and total cash to close for each.
Ask what your reserves look like
after closing in each scenario. Aim to have something left.
Check Oregon Bond eligibility
against the income and purchase price limits for the county you are shopping in.
Get PMI quoted at your actual credit score
before assuming it is expensive. The pricing spread across credit tiers is wide.
Decide based on the full picture
, not a number you heard from a relative in 1994.

Bri Lindley, Mortgage Loan Officer with The Lindley Team at Movement Mortgage (NMLS #1367416), works with buyers across the Portland metro on exactly these comparisons. This article is general education, not individualized advice or an offer of credit.

faqs.question: Do I really need 20% down to buy a house in Portland?
faqs.answer: No. Conventional loans go as low as 3% down for qualifying first-time buyers and 5% for many others, FHA allows 3.5%, and VA and USDA allow zero down for eligible borrowers. The 20% figure exists because that is the point where conventional mortgage insurance is no longer required — not because it is a legal or lending requirement.

faqs.question: What is the Oregon Bond Residential Loan Program and who qualifies?
faqs.answer: It is a state program through Oregon Housing and Community Services offering either a reduced interest rate or cash assistance toward down payment and closing costs. Eligibility depends on household income limits and purchase price limits that vary by county, and it generally targets buyers who have not owned a primary residence in the past three years. Only participating lenders can originate these loans.

faqs.question: Is it smarter to put 10% down instead of 20%?
faqs.answer: For many buyers, yes. At 10% down, mortgage insurance factors are lower than at 5% down, the loan is smaller than at minimum down payment, and you keep roughly half your cash available for repairs, reserves, and emergencies. Since conventional PMI cancels once you reach 80% equity, the added cost is temporary rather than permanent.

faqs.question: Will a seller reject my offer if I'm not putting 20% down?
faqs.answer: Sellers care primarily about whether the transaction closes on time, not about your down payment percentage. A fully underwritten preapproval, a realistic timeline, and a responsive lender do more to strengthen an offer than a larger down payment with weak documentation. In competitive situations, terms like inspection approach and closing flexibility typically carry more weight.

title: A Beginner's Guide to Understanding Mortgage Refinance Options
excerpt: If the term 'refinance' sounds like it belongs to another language, you're not alone.

seo.metaDescription: If the term 'refinance' sounds like it belongs to another language, you're not alone.

children.text: Three different people can say "I want to refinance" and mean three completely different things. One wants a lower payment. One wants to pull cash out of a Northeast Portland bungalow that has appreciated since 2016. One wants their ex-spouse's name off the loan before the divorce decree is final.
Same word. Three very different transactions, with different paperwork, different costs, and different reasons they might be a bad idea.
So before you can decide whether refinancing makes sense for you, it helps to know what's actually on the menu. This is the menu.
What a Refinance Actually Is

A refinance is a new mortgage that pays off your old mortgage. You are not modifying your existing loan or negotiating with your current servicer. You are getting a brand-new loan, with a new note, a new rate, a new term, and new closing costs, and that new loan wires money to your old lender to zero it out.

That distinction matters more than people expect. Because it's a new loan, you go through underwriting again. Income documentation, credit, appraisal or an appraisal waiver, title work, the whole thing.

It also means the clock restarts. A new 30-year loan is 30 years from the day you sign, even if you were 7 years into your last one. That's not automatically bad, but it's the detail most people forget to account for.
The Rate-and-Term Refinance
This is the plain vanilla version. You replace your existing loan with a new one for roughly the same balance, changing the
rate
, the
term
, or both. No cash comes back to you at closing beyond a small incidental amount.
People use rate-and-term refinances to:
Lower the interest rate, when market conditions and their own credit profile make that possible
Shorten the term, moving from a 30-year to a 20- or 15-year
Lengthen the term to reduce the monthly payment, accepting more total interest
Move from an adjustable-rate mortgage to a fixed rate for predictability
Whether any of these is worth doing depends entirely on current market conditions and the specific loan you have now. A rate-and-term refi is a tool, not a strategy.
The Cash-Out Refinance
A cash-out refinance replaces your loan with a larger one and hands you the difference at closing, minus costs.
On a
hypothetical
home appraised at $600,000 with a
hypothetical

remaining balance of $300,000, a borrower taking a new loan of $390,000 would receive roughly $90,000 before closing costs. That $90,000 isn't free money. It's borrowed against the house, repaid over the loan term, with interest.

Common uses include home renovation, consolidating higher-interest debt, funding a business, or covering an equity buyout in a divorce. Lenders generally price cash-out loans differently than rate-and-term loans, and there are limits on how much of your home's value you can borrow against. Those limits vary by loan program and by occupancy — a primary residence and a rental in Gresham are not treated the same way.

The honest caution: using a 30-year mortgage to pay off a credit card converts a short, expensive debt into a long, cheaper-per-month one. Sometimes that's the right call. Sometimes it just moves the problem somewhere it can quietly grow.
Streamline Refinances
If your current loan is government-backed, there may be a simplified path.
FHA Streamline
For existing FHA loans. Reduced documentation, and in many cases no new appraisal. Designed for rate-and-term changes only, not cash out.
VA Interest Rate Reduction Refinance Loan (IRRRL)
For existing VA loans. Similar concept — less paperwork, no cash out, must generally produce a tangible benefit for the borrower.
USDA Streamlined Assist

For existing USDA loans in eligible rural areas. Parts of Clackamas, Columbia, and Yamhill counties include USDA-eligible tracts, so this comes up more around the Portland metro edges than people assume.
Streamline programs still have costs, and the rules on what qualifies as a "net tangible benefit" are specific. They are simpler, not free.
Removing a Borrower From the Loan
This one deserves its own section because it's badly misunderstood.

A divorce decree can order that one spouse takes the house. It does not remove the other spouse from the mortgage. The lender wasn't party to that agreement. Until the loan is refinanced or otherwise released, both names stay on the debt, and both credit reports keep reflecting it.
An
equity buyout refinance

does two jobs at once: it puts the loan in one person's name and pulls out enough equity to pay the other party their share. Depending on how the divorce documents are written and the timing involved, this may be treated under different guidelines than a standard cash-out — which can matter for pricing and for how much equity is accessible.

The order of operations matters here. Property settlement language written before anyone talks to a lender frequently creates a plan that can't actually be financed. Talking to a Certified Divorce Lending Professional while the agreement is still in draft is a lot cheaper than amending it later.
What All Refinances Have in Common
Regardless of type, expect the following.
Closing costs.
Origination, title, escrow, recording, appraisal if required. These are real dollars, whether you pay them upfront, roll them into the balance, or accept a higher rate in exchange for a credit.
Underwriting.
Income, assets, credit, and property all get reviewed again.
A new amortization schedule.
Early payments are interest-heavy again.
Oregon-specific items.

Recording fees vary by county — Multnomah, Washington, and Clackamas each set their own. Oregon's property tax cycle, with statements in October and the discount for paying in full by mid-November, can also affect escrow setup and how much cash you bring to closing.
There's no version of a refinance where the costs disappear. The question is whether what you get back is worth what you pay.
Which One Fits Which Situation
A rough map, not a prescription:
Payment is straining the budget
→ rate-and-term with a longer term, understanding the total-interest tradeoff
Want to be debt-free faster
→ shorter term, if the higher payment is genuinely sustainable
Need funds for a specific purpose
→ cash-out, with a clear plan for the money
Adjustable loan making you nervous
→ fixed-rate rate-and-term
Existing FHA, VA, or USDA loan, no cash needed
→ check the streamline option first
Divorce or separation
→ equity buyout or name-removal refinance, coordinated with your attorney
What to Do Next
Pull your current mortgage statement and find four numbers: balance, rate, remaining term, and whether you're paying mortgage insurance.
Write down the actual goal in one sentence. "Lower payment" and "pay it off sooner" are opposite goals and require opposite loans.
Estimate your equity using a realistic value for your neighborhood, not a Zestimate you liked.
Talk to a licensed loan officer who will run your specific numbers and show you the breakeven math before you commit to anything.

Whether a refinance makes sense right now depends on where rates sit, what your existing loan looks like, and how long you plan to keep the house. Nobody can answer that from a blog post — including this one.

faqs.question: How soon after buying a house can I refinance?
faqs.answer: It depends on your loan type, and there is often a waiting period. Some programs require six months of payments before a refinance, and cash-out transactions frequently carry longer seasoning requirements. Conventional rate-and-term loans are sometimes more flexible. The practical question is usually not whether you are allowed to, but whether enough has changed since closing to make it worth the costs.

faqs.question: Does refinancing hurt my credit score?
faqs.answer: There is usually a small, temporary dip. A refinance involves a hard credit inquiry and creates a new account while closing an old one, which can shorten your average account age. Credit scoring models generally treat multiple mortgage inquiries within a short shopping window as a single event, so comparing lenders over a couple of weeks does not multiply the impact.

faqs.question: Can I refinance if my ex is still on the mortgage?
faqs.answer: Yes, and that is often exactly the point of the refinance. A divorce decree assigning the house to one spouse does not remove the other from the mortgage, because the lender was not a party to that agreement. A refinance in one name is the usual mechanism for a release. Qualifying happens on the remaining borrower's income and credit alone.

faqs.question: What does it cost to refinance in Oregon?
faqs.answer: Costs vary by loan amount, lender, and county, so there is no single figure. Expect lender fees, title and escrow charges, possibly an appraisal, and county recording fees that differ between Multnomah, Washington, and Clackamas. You can pay these in cash, roll them into the balance, or accept a higher rate in exchange for a lender credit. Each choice shifts cost rather than removing it.

title: 3 Surprisingly Simple Ways to Stop Paying Private Mortgage Insurance (PMI)
excerpt: It's no secret that owning real estate is one of the best ways to build wealth.

seo.metaDescription: It's no secret that owning real estate is one of the best ways to build wealth.

children.text: A homeowner in Southeast Portland called me last spring, annoyed. She had been paying $187 a month in private mortgage insurance for four years — roughly $9,000 — and had just realized her home was probably worth enough that she did not have to anymore. Nobody had told her. Nobody was going to.

That is the thing about PMI. It is the only line item on your mortgage statement that exists solely to protect the lender, and the only one that can disappear entirely if you pay attention at the right moment. Your servicer is required to drop it at a certain point, but "required at a certain point" and "as soon as you qualify" are very different dates.
Here is what PMI actually is, and the three realistic ways to get out from under it.
What PMI Is and Why You Have It

Private mortgage insurance is a policy that reimburses the lender if you default. You pay the premium. You get none of the protection. It is generally required on conventional loans when your down payment is less than 20% of the purchase price.

It is not a scam and it is not a punishment. PMI is the mechanism that lets people buy homes with 3% or 5% down instead of waiting years to save 20%. In a market like Portland's, where prices have historically outpaced most people's savings rate, buying earlier with PMI has often been the better financial move than waiting. But once it has done its job, there is no reason to keep paying for it.
A few important distinctions before we go further:
PMI is a conventional loan term.

FHA loans carry Mortgage Insurance Premium (MIP), which follows entirely different rules and, on most modern FHA loans with less than 10% down, lasts the life of the loan. Getting rid of FHA MIP usually means refinancing into a conventional loan.
VA loans have no monthly mortgage insurance at all.
There is a one-time funding fee instead.
Lender-paid PMI (LPMI)
is baked into your interest rate rather than billed monthly. It cannot be removed by request. Refinancing is the only exit.
Everything below applies to borrower-paid PMI on a conventional loan.
Path One: Reach 80% by Paying the Loan Down
The Homeowners Protection Act of 1998 gives you two specific rights on most conventional loans for a primary residence.
At 80% loan-to-value, you can request cancellation.
Once your principal balance reaches 80% of the *original* value — the lesser of purchase price or original appraised value — you may submit a written request to your servicer to cancel PMI.
At 78% loan-to-value, cancellation is automatic.
Your servicer must terminate PMI on its own, based on the original amortization schedule, with no request from you.

Note the gap. That 2% difference is a real amount of money, and it is on you to claim it. On a hypothetical $400,000 original value, 80% is $320,000 and 78% is $312,000. Waiting for automatic termination could easily mean paying an extra year of premiums.
To qualify for a request at 80%, servicers typically require that you:
Are current on payments and have a clean recent payment history
Have no second lien on the property
Submit the request
in writing

You can also get there faster. Extra principal payments accelerate the date you hit 80%. If you have a lump sum — a bonus, a tax refund — applying it to principal specifically to cross the 80% threshold can pay for itself quickly.
Path Two: Removal Based on Appreciation
This is the path most Portland homeowners overlook, and it is the one with the biggest potential payoff.

If your home's value has increased, your current loan-to-value ratio may already be well under 80% even though your loan balance has barely moved. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac both allow PMI removal based on a
current
value rather than the original one — but they impose seasoning requirements, and this is where people get tripped up.
The Seasoning Rules Are Investor-Specific
The requirements vary depending on who owns your loan, and they change from time to time. As a general shape of the rules:
If the loan is relatively new (commonly cited as fewer than two years), appreciation-based removal is typically not permitted at all unless the increase came from documented improvements.
Between roughly two and five years of seasoning, investors generally require a lower LTV threshold than 80% — often closer to 75%.
After about five years, the standard 80% threshold usually applies.
Do not rely on those numbers as gospel.

Call your servicer, ask specifically which investor owns your loan, and ask them to state their current appreciation-based cancellation requirements in writing. This is a five-minute phone call that people put off for years.

You will almost certainly need to pay for a new valuation — typically a Broker Price Opinion or a full appraisal, ordered by the servicer, not by you. Expect a few hundred dollars. If it clears the threshold, that cost is usually recovered in a handful of months of premiums.
Why This Matters in the Portland Metro

Home values in the Portland metro have not moved uniformly. A house in Multnomah County near a stalled commercial corridor may have appreciated very differently from a comparable house in Washington County near the tech employment centers, or in Clackamas County where inventory patterns differ again. If you bought with a small down payment and your neighborhood has appreciated meaningfully, run the numbers before assuming you are stuck.
Path Three: Refinance

Refinancing replaces your existing loan with a new one. If the new loan is at or below 80% of the current appraised value, the new loan simply does not have PMI. There is no request, no seasoning rule to argue about, no servicer discretion.
This is the only option for:
FHA loans with lifetime MIP
Lender-paid PMI
Situations where your servicer's appreciation rules are unworkable

The tradeoff is honest and worth stating plainly: refinancing means new closing costs and, potentially, a different interest rate than the one you currently have. If your existing rate is lower than what is available when you refinance, dropping PMI may not offset the change in interest cost. That math has to be run for your specific loan — not assumed.

The question is never "should I refinance to drop PMI." It is "does the total cost of the new loan, including closing costs and the new rate, come out ahead of my current loan including PMI, over the period I actually plan to keep this house."
If you are in Oregon and originally financed through the
Oregon Bond Residential Loan Program
, check your loan terms carefully before refinancing. Bond program loans carry specific structures, and refinancing out of one has consequences worth understanding first.
A Note on What Nobody Will Tell You
Your servicer has no obligation to inform you that appreciation-based removal exists. They will follow the automatic 78% rule because the law requires it. Everything before that is your move to make.

Set a calendar reminder. Once a year, pull your current principal balance from your statement, get a rough sense of your home's value, and do the division. If the result is under 0.80, make a phone call.
What to Do Next
Find your original value and current principal balance.
Both are on your closing documents and your latest mortgage statement.
Call your servicer and ask two questions:
who owns my loan, and what are your current requirements for PMI cancellation based on current value?
Get the answer in writing
before you pay for any valuation.
If you have an FHA loan or lender-paid PMI,
skip straight to evaluating a refinance, because the request path is not available to you.

If you want a second set of eyes on the math before you spend money on an appraisal, that is a conversation worth having. This is general education, not advice about your specific loan — your situation deserves an actual look at your actual numbers.

faqs.question: How do I know if I'm even paying PMI right now?
faqs.answer: Look at your monthly mortgage statement for a line labeled PMI, MI, or mortgage insurance. If your payment is escrowed, it may be bundled into the total, so check the itemized breakdown or your original closing disclosure. If you put down less than 20% on a conventional loan, you almost certainly have it. FHA loans show it as MIP instead.

faqs.question: Can my lender just say no when I ask them to remove it?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you don't meet the conditions. At 80% of original value with a clean payment history and no second lien, a conventional servicer generally must honor a written request. For appreciation-based removal, the servicer has more discretion because investor seasoning rules apply and the new valuation has to support the number. Ask for any denial in writing with the specific reason.

faqs.question: Is it worth paying for an appraisal just to drop PMI?
faqs.answer: Often, but do the math first. If you're paying a hypothetical $200 a month in PMI and an appraisal costs $600, you'd recover the cost in three months of premiums — assuming the value comes in high enough. The risk is paying for a valuation that doesn't clear the threshold. Get a realistic value estimate before ordering anything.

faqs.question: Does PMI go away on its own if I never do anything?
faqs.answer: On most conventional loans for a primary residence, yes — automatically at 78% of original value based on the original amortization schedule. But that's the slowest possible path. It ignores appreciation entirely and it ignores any extra principal you've paid. Most people who wait for automatic termination pay more than they had to.

title: A Comprehensive Guide to the Ins and Outs of Private Mortgage Insurance (PMI)
excerpt: Chances are, you've heard some buzz about the record low interest rates.

seo.metaDescription: Chances are, you've heard some buzz about the record low interest rates.

children.text: A buyer in Southeast Portland puts 10% down on a 1920s bungalow. Their loan estimate includes a line for private mortgage insurance, and their first reaction is the one almost everyone has: I am paying for insurance that protects the bank, not me, and I did not ask for it.

Both halves of that are true. The part that gets left out is that PMI is what let them buy the house three years earlier than they otherwise could have, and that it is removable — sometimes automatically, sometimes on request, sometimes years ahead of schedule.
Here is the full picture, including the parts lenders tend to gloss over.
What PMI Actually Does

Private mortgage insurance is a policy the lender requires when a conventional loan exceeds 80% of the property's value. If the loan defaults and the foreclosure sale does not cover the balance, the insurer covers part of the lender's loss.
You pay the premium. The lender is the beneficiary. That is genuinely how it works, and there is no point pretending otherwise.

The reason it exists at all is that without it, conventional lending below 20% down would be far more restricted. PMI is the mechanism that makes a 3% or 5% down conventional loan possible. It is a toll, not a penalty.
One important distinction:
PMI is a conventional loan product.

FHA loans carry a different thing called MIP, VA loans carry a funding fee instead, and USDA loans have their own fee structure. The rules for removing them are not the same, which trips up a lot of borrowers.
The Four Ways You Can Pay It
Most borrowers are shown one option and assume it is the only one.
Borrower-paid monthly (BPMI).
The most common structure. A premium is added to your monthly payment and it can be cancelled once you hit certain equity thresholds. This is the default for most people.
Single premium.
You pay the whole thing upfront at closing, either in cash or financed into the loan. Lowers the monthly payment. Generally not refundable if you sell or refinance early.
Lender-paid (LPMI).

The lender covers the premium in exchange for a permanently higher interest rate. No separate PMI line item, which people like. The catch is that the higher rate does not go away when you cross 80% equity — only refinancing removes it.
Split premium.
A partial upfront payment plus a smaller monthly amount. A middle path that occasionally prices out well.

Which one wins depends almost entirely on how long you keep the loan. Single premium and LPMI tend to favor long holds; monthly BPMI tends to favor shorter ones or situations where you expect equity to build quickly.
What Determines Your PMI Cost
PMI is not one price. It is priced off a matrix, and the same buyer can get materially different quotes by changing one input.
The main factors:
Loan-to-value ratio.
95% LTV costs more than 90%, which costs more than 85%.
Credit score.
This is the big one. PMI pricing is highly credit-sensitive, more so than interest rate pricing in many cases.
Debt-to-income ratio.
Higher DTI can push you into a worse tier.
Loan term.
Shorter terms generally carry lower factors.
Occupancy and property type.
Primary residences price better than second homes; single-family better than multi-unit.
Number of borrowers and loan purpose.
Both feed the matrix.
To illustrate the math without quoting a real price: on a
hypothetical $400,000 loan with a hypothetical annual PMI factor of 0.50%
, the premium would be $2,000 per year, or about $167 per month. Change the factor to a hypothetical 0.90% and the same loan runs $3,600 per year, roughly $300 per month.

That spread is why it is worth asking your loan officer to quote PMI at your actual credit score and to tell you what a modest score improvement would do. Sometimes 20 points is worth chasing before you apply.
How PMI Goes Away
This is the part worth writing down, because servicers are not in the habit of volunteering it.
Under the federal
Homeowners Protection Act
, for most conventional loans on a primary residence:
At 78% LTV based on the original amortization schedule
, the servicer must cancel PMI automatically, provided you are current on payments. This is scheduled — no request needed.
At 80% LTV based on the original value
, you may request cancellation in writing. The servicer can require a good payment history, no junior liens, and sometimes evidence the value has not declined.
At the midpoint of the amortization period
, PMI terminates for loans that have not reached those thresholds.
Separately, most investors allow
appreciation-based removal

. If your home has gained value, you can request that the servicer order a new valuation and cancel PMI based on current value rather than original value. Requirements vary — commonly a minimum seasoning period of two years, sometimes five, with different LTV thresholds depending on how long you have owned it.
For Portland-area homeowners who bought during a period of rising values, this is the option most often left on the table. It costs an appraisal fee and a phone call.
Refinancing also removes PMI, but that trades one variable for another. If your current rate is favorable, refinancing purely to escape PMI can cost more than it saves.
PMI Versus FHA Mortgage Insurance
This comparison decides a lot of loan choices, so it deserves its own section.
FHA loans carry an
upfront mortgage insurance premium
financed into the loan plus an
annual MIP
paid monthly. Critically, when an FHA borrower puts less than 10% down, the annual MIP generally stays for the life of the loan. It does not fall off at 78%.

Conventional PMI is cancellable. That single difference means a borrower with strong credit is often better served by a low-down-payment conventional loan than by FHA, even if the FHA rate looks more attractive at first glance.

Borrowers with lower credit scores frequently see the opposite result, because conventional PMI pricing punishes weaker credit harder than FHA does. There is no universal answer — it is a side-by-side comparison every time.
Is PMI Worth Paying?
The honest framing is opportunity cost. On a
hypothetical $500,000 Portland-area purchase
, 20% down is $100,000 and 10% down is $50,000. If saving that additional $50,000 takes three more years, PMI is the price of not waiting three years.
Whether that trade is worth it depends on rent in the meantime, what home values do, what rates do, and what else you would do with the cash. Nobody can promise which way those move.
What is knowable is the cost of the toll and the exit path off it.
What To Do Next
Ask for PMI quoted at your actual credit score
, and ask what the next credit tier up would cost.
Request a side-by-side
of monthly BPMI, single premium, and lender-paid on the same scenario.
If you already have PMI
, find your original amortization schedule and mark the month you hit 80% and 78%.
If your home has appreciated
, call your servicer and ask about their appreciation-based cancellation policy and seasoning requirement.
Compare conventional-with-PMI against FHA
before assuming one is cheaper.

Bri Lindley, Mortgage Loan Officer with The Lindley Team at Movement Mortgage (NMLS #1367416), can run those comparisons for your specific numbers. Everything above is general education, not individualized advice.

faqs.question: How do I get rid of PMI on my mortgage?
faqs.answer: You can request cancellation in writing once your balance reaches 80% of the home's original value, and most conventional loans terminate PMI automatically at 78% based on the original amortization schedule. You may also be able to remove it early based on appreciation by asking your servicer to order a new valuation, though seasoning requirements and LTV thresholds vary by investor. Refinancing is a third path.

faqs.question: Does PMI ever go away on an FHA loan?
faqs.answer: Usually not, if you put less than 10% down. FHA annual mortgage insurance premiums generally remain for the life of the loan in that case, unlike conventional PMI, which is cancellable. Borrowers who put 10% or more down on FHA typically see MIP drop after 11 years. Many FHA borrowers eventually refinance into a conventional loan specifically to shed the premium once they have enough equity.

faqs.question: How much does PMI cost per month?
faqs.answer: PMI is priced from a matrix, so it varies widely based on your credit score, loan-to-value, debt-to-income, and property type. As an illustration only, a hypothetical $400,000 loan with a hypothetical 0.50% annual factor would run about $167 per month, while a hypothetical 0.90% factor on the same loan would run about $300. Ask your loan officer for a quote at your actual credit score.

faqs.question: Is it better to pay PMI monthly or upfront?
faqs.answer: It depends mostly on how long you expect to keep the loan. Monthly PMI costs nothing at closing and cancels once you reach the equity thresholds, which suits shorter holds or fast-appreciating situations. A single upfront premium lowers the monthly payment but is generally non-refundable if you sell or refinance early. Ask for both structures quoted side by side before choosing.

children.text: Two buyers write offers on the same three-bedroom in Beaverton in the same week. Same purchase price. Same down payment. Same loan program. One of them ends up with a principal-and-interest payment noticeably higher than the other, for the entire 30 years.
Nothing about the house changed. The only variable was the interest rate each one ended up with, and the handful of decisions that produced it.

Most people treat the interest rate as a number that gets handed to them, like a weather forecast. It is closer to a price quote, and prices depend on inputs. Here is how the whole thing actually works.
What an Interest Rate Actually Is
A mortgage interest rate is the annual cost of borrowing money, expressed as a percentage of the balance you still owe. You are essentially renting capital, and the rate is the rent.
That is different from
APR

, which shows up next to the rate on every disclosure and confuses nearly everyone. APR folds certain lender fees and financing costs into a single annualized number so you can compare offers that have different fee structures. The rate determines your payment. The APR is a comparison tool.

Two loans can carry the same rate and different APRs, which usually means one has more upfront cost baked in. Two loans can also carry different rates and similar APRs. Neither number tells the whole story alone.
How a Rate Turns Into a Monthly Payment
Mortgages are amortized, which means each payment covers the interest that accrued that month first, and whatever is left over reduces the balance.
Take a
hypothetical $400,000 loan at a hypothetical 6% fixed rate over 30 years
. Principal and interest would run roughly $2,398 per month. In the very first month, about $2,000 of that goes to interest and only about $398 touches the balance.
Run the same hypothetical loan at
instead and principal and interest lands near $2,661. That is roughly $263 a month for the same house, the same keys, the same everything.

These are illustrations, not quotes. Nobody can tell you what rate you would receive without looking at your actual file. But the mechanic holds: a one-point difference in rate on a mid-size loan tends to move the payment by a few hundred dollars, and the effect compounds over the life of the loan.

The flip side is that the balance shrinks slowly at first and then accelerates. By year 15 of that hypothetical loan, the split has moved substantially toward principal. This is why extra principal payments made early do more work than the same dollars applied later.
The Rest of Your Payment Is Not Interest at All

When people compare payments, they often compare different things. Principal and interest is one slice. Most Portland-area borrowers also escrow for property taxes and homeowners insurance, and some carry mortgage insurance.
Oregon property taxes are worth understanding here. Because of Measure 50, your tax bill is generally tied to an
assessed value
that grows on a capped schedule, not directly to what you paid for the house. That means two neighboring homes with similar market values can carry meaningfully different tax bills.

It also means effective tax rates vary across the metro. Multnomah, Washington, and Clackamas counties each layer in different local levies and bond measures, and rates differ again between districts inside a single county. A payment estimate built on a countywide average can be off by a real amount once the actual parcel is pulled.
If a lender quotes you a payment and it seems suspiciously low compared to another quote, check whether taxes, insurance, and any mortgage insurance are actually in there.
What Moves Mortgage Rates
The most common misconception is that the Federal Reserve sets mortgage rates. It does not. The Fed sets the federal funds rate, which is an overnight bank-to-bank rate.
Long-term mortgage rates are driven mostly by the
mortgage-backed securities market

. Investors buy bundles of home loans, and what they are willing to pay for those bundles determines what lenders can offer. The 10-year Treasury yield tends to move in a similar direction, which is why it gets used as a rough shorthand.

What those investors care about is largely inflation expectations, the strength of the labor market, and how much supply of new bonds is coming. Inflation erodes the value of fixed future payments, so rising inflation expectations generally push rates up.
Practically: rates can move on an economic report at 5:30 a.m. Pacific and move again by mid-morning. A quote from Tuesday is not a Thursday quote.
What You Actually Control
You do not control the bond market. You do control a surprising number of the inputs that price your specific loan.
Credit score.
Pricing moves in tiers. Being a few points below a threshold can cost you, and a few points is sometimes fixable.
Loan-to-value.
How much you put down affects both mortgage insurance and rate pricing.
Loan program.
Conventional, FHA, VA, and jumbo loans price differently, and the one with the lowest rate is not automatically the cheapest overall once fees and mortgage insurance are counted.
Occupancy and property type.
A primary residence prices differently than a rental. A condo prices differently than a detached house.
Lock period.
Longer locks generally cost more, because the lender is holding risk longer.
Points and credits.
You can pay upfront to lower the rate, or accept a higher rate in exchange for a credit toward closing costs.

On points, the only question that matters is the breakeven. If paying an additional amount upfront lowers your payment by some amount per month, divide the cost by the monthly savings to get the number of months to break even. Then ask honestly whether you expect to keep the loan that long.
Rate Versus Price in the Portland Metro
Buyers often fixate on the rate and ignore the loan amount, which is the other half of the equation. Your payment is a function of both.

In practical terms, when financing costs rise, buyer competition often cools and negotiating room can open up — seller-paid closing costs, repair credits, rate buydowns. When financing costs fall, competition tends to intensify and those concessions get harder to win.

The rate on your loan is also the only major term that can be changed later without moving. Purchase price is permanent. That asymmetry is worth sitting with, though refinancing depends on future market conditions that nobody can predict or promise.
What To Do Next
Pull your actual credit
through a lender, not just a free app. Consumer scores and mortgage scores are frequently different models.
Ask for a full payment breakdown
, not a principal-and-interest number — taxes, insurance, HOA, and any mortgage insurance included.
Get the property tax figure for the specific address
you are considering, not a county average.
Compare two or three scenarios side by side
at different down payments and loan programs before you decide what to offer.
Have a conversation about your timeline.
How long you plan to hold the loan changes whether points, a longer lock, or a different program makes sense.

Bri Lindley, Mortgage Loan Officer with The Lindley Team at Movement Mortgage (NMLS #1367416), works with Portland-area buyers on exactly this kind of scenario modeling. Every situation is different, and the numbers here are educational illustrations rather than an offer of credit.

faqs.question: How much does a 1% change in interest rate affect my mortgage payment?
faqs.answer: As a rule of thumb, one percentage point moves principal and interest by roughly $60 to $70 per month for every $100,000 borrowed on a 30-year fixed loan. On a hypothetical $400,000 loan, going from a hypothetical 6% to 7% moves principal and interest from about $2,398 to about $2,661. The exact figure depends on loan amount and term, and these are illustrations, not quotes.

faqs.question: Does the Federal Reserve set mortgage rates?
faqs.answer: No. The Fed sets the federal funds rate, an overnight rate between banks. Mortgage rates are driven mainly by the mortgage-backed securities market, where investors decide what they will pay for bundles of home loans. Fed policy influences that market indirectly through inflation and growth expectations, which is why mortgage rates sometimes move opposite the direction people expect after a Fed announcement.

faqs.question: What's the difference between interest rate and APR on a mortgage?
faqs.answer: The interest rate determines your monthly principal and interest payment; the APR is a comparison figure that rolls certain lender fees and financing costs into an annualized percentage. Two loans with identical rates can have different APRs if one carries higher upfront costs. Use the rate to understand your payment and the APR as one input when comparing offers, alongside the actual itemized fees.

faqs.question: Why is my mortgage payment higher than the rate calculator said?
faqs.answer: Most online calculators show only principal and interest. Your actual payment usually also includes property taxes, homeowners insurance, mortgage insurance if applicable, and HOA dues if the property has them. In the Portland metro, property taxes vary by county and tax district because of how Oregon assesses value, so a countywide average can be well off for a specific address.
